`--store`, `--write`, `--data` and the `data`, `backends` and `write` keys of `atlas.server.json` are gone; a
configuration file that still has one of the keys is refused with a message that says so.

**It fails fast and loud.** Before anything listens, the server checks every variable, then proves the bucket is
usable (lists it, writes and deletes a scratch object) and reads the user state. If any step fails it prints a banner
that lists **every** variable with `[MISSING]`, `[INVALID]`, `[ok]` or `[not set]`, says why storage is required (and
what S3 answered, when S3 was reached), never prints a secret, and exits with status **2**:

```text
==============================================================================
  ATLAS CANNOT START: S3 STORAGE IS NOT USABLE
==============================================================================
  Why:    the S3 configuration is missing or invalid.
  Reason: Atlas stores ALL reports and ALL user state (the garbage collection policy and saved
          settings) in S3-compatible object storage, and nowhere else. There is no local-disk,
          in-memory or database fallback, so the server refuses to start without working S3.

  Required environment variables:
  [MISSING] ATLAS_S3_ENDPOINT           S3 API endpoint of the object storage service
  [ok]      ATLAS_S3_BUCKET             Bucket that holds reports and user state; it must already exist
  [INVALID] ATLAS_S3_REGION             must be lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, like eu-west-1
  …
  Fix these 2: ATLAS_S3_ENDPOINT, ATLAS_S3_REGION
```

Credentials that S3 rejects, a bucket that does not exist and a user state object that cannot be read stop the
server in the same way, with the answer from S3 in the banner. `atlas dev` behaves the same.

## User state and garbage collection

Everything a person using Atlas has chosen is **user state**: one JSON document, `server/state.json` under
`ATLAS_S3_PREFIX`, in the same bucket as the reports. It is never kept on the server's disk or in the browser.

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "gc": { "enabled": true, "maxAgeDays": 90, "keepLatest": 20, "intervalHours": 24 },
  "settings": { "refreshSeconds": 30 }
}
```

(published as [`user-state.schema.json`](https://github.com/crvouga/atlas/blob/main/packages/schema/schemas/user-state.schema.json))

- **`gc` is the garbage collection policy**, defined in the Atlas UI (**Settings**, `/admin`, *Garbage collection*) and
  read by the server **from S3 every time it collects**, so a saved policy applies at the next pass without a restart.
- **`settings`** are the report and live-run settings saved from the same page. They apply at the next start, below
  `atlas.server.json`, the environment and the flags in precedence.
- A document that does not exist is an empty state; one that exists but cannot be parsed stops the server and is
  never overwritten.

**No policy saved yet.** Atlas is deletion-free until someone says otherwise: with no `gc` in the document,
garbage collection is **off and nothing is ever deleted**. The server says so at start, the API answers
`saved: false, policy: null`, the page shows a "No policy has been saved yet" notice with suggested values that take
effect only after you turn collection on and save, and `POST /api/settings/gc/run` answers 409. There is no
fallback to a file, an environment variable or built-in numbers.

**What a policy deletes.** With `enabled: true`, every `intervalHours` (and shortly after start) the server applies the
policy to every project. It deletes a report layer only when all of these hold:

1. the server has read it and every check it carries has been replaced by a newer layer, so it no longer decides any
   result (deleting it cannot change the report);
2. it was recorded more than `maxAgeDays` days ago;
3. it is not one of the newest `keepLatest` layers of its project.

The layer's catalog entry goes first (so nothing visible points at a missing manifest), then its manifest, then the
captured files (screenshots, logs, …) that no remaining layer refers to; if any remaining layer cannot be read, no
file is deleted. Specs, runs and commit inventories are never touched, and a layer that failed to load, that
`include` hides, or that still decides a result is never a candidate. Because a deleted layer is also removed from the
test history, history older than the policy allows is gone after the next start. One narrow race remains: a publisher
that reuses a stored file at the very moment the last layer that used it is deleted can end up with a layer that
points at a missing file; keep `maxAgeDays` well above the time uploads take.

**Editing it.** `GET /api/settings/gc` and `PUT /api/settings/gc` (admin, with `If-Match` the revision that was read,
same-origin in browsers) read and save the policy; `POST /api/settings/gc/run` applies it now, and
`POST /api/settings/gc/run?dryRun=1` only counts what would go. A save that races another is refused with 409. The
revision is the SHA-256 of the stored document, so saving the policy and saving settings invalidate each other's
revision: reload, then save. An object store has no conditional writes, so run one server per bucket.

## Configuration

Everything but the [S3 storage](#required-s3-storage) has a default. Settings come from the settings saved in S3 (the lowest layer), then
`atlas.server.json` (or `--config <file>` / `ATLAS_CONFIG`), then environment variables, then flags; a later one
wins. A mistake (an unknown key, a short token, listening beyond this machine without tokens)
is said in words and the server does not start. The file has a published
[JSON Schema](https://github.com/crvouga/atlas/blob/main/packages/schema/schemas/server-config.schema.json)
(`@crvouga/atlas/schemas/server-config.schema.json`).

```json
{
  "$schema": "./node_modules/@crvouga/atlas/packages/schema/schemas/server-config.schema.json",
  "host": "0.0.0.0",
  "port": 8080,
  "auth": {
    "tokens": [
      { "name": "ci", "role": "publish", "tokenEnv": "ATLAS_CI_TOKEN" },
      { "name": "dashboard", "role": "read", "tokenEnv": "ATLAS_DASHBOARD_TOKEN" }
    ]
  },
  "include": { "branches": ["main"], "ignoreModified": true },
  "refreshSeconds": 10,
  "limits": { "maxObjectMiB": 256, "maxJsonMiB": 32, "maxStreams": 500 }
}
```

<!-- generated:server-settings -->
| Setting | File key | Flag | Environment | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| S3 endpoint URL (**required**) | `storage.s3.endpoint` |  | `ATLAS_S3_ENDPOINT` | **none: the server refuses to start** |
| Bucket for all reports and user state (**required**) | `storage.s3.bucket` |  | `ATLAS_S3_BUCKET` | **none: the server refuses to start** |
| Bucket region (**required**) | `storage.s3.region` |  | `ATLAS_S3_REGION` | **none: the server refuses to start** |
| Access key id (**required**) | `storage.s3.accessKeyId` |  | `ATLAS_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID` | **none: the server refuses to start** |
| Secret access key (**required**) | `storage.s3.secretAccessKey` |  | `ATLAS_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` | **none: the server refuses to start** |
| Folder in the bucket for everything Atlas writes (optional) | `storage.s3.prefix` |  | `ATLAS_S3_PREFIX` | the bucket root |
| Path-style bucket addressing (`0` for virtual-hosted) (optional) | `storage.s3.pathStyle` |  | `ATLAS_S3_PATH_STYLE` | yes |
| Session token for temporary credentials (optional) | `storage.s3.sessionToken` |  | `ATLAS_S3_SESSION_TOKEN` | none |
| Address to listen on | `host` | `--host <address>` | `ATLAS_HOST`, `HOST` | `127.0.0.1` |
| Port (`0` picks a free one) | `port` | `--port <n>` | `ATLAS_PORT`, `PORT` | `8080` |
| The built client | `site` | `--site <dir>` | `ATLAS_SITE` | `./atlas-site`, else built once |
| Whose specs the report is laid over | `outlineBranch` | `--outline-branch <branch>` | `ATLAS_OUTLINE_BRANCH` | `main`, then `master`, then the newest |
| Only layers recorded on these branches take part | `include.branches` | `--branch <name>` (repeatable) | `ATLAS_ONLY_BRANCH` | all |
| Leave out layers from modified checkouts and unknown origins | `include.ignoreModified` | `--ignore-modified` | `ATLAS_IGNORE_MODIFIED` | no |
| How often (seconds) the backends are looked at for layers written by something else | `refreshSeconds` | `--refresh <seconds>` | `ATLAS_REFRESH_SECONDS` | `10` |
| Let anyone look, not upload | `auth.anonymousRead` | `--anonymous-read` | `ATLAS_ANONYMOUS_READ` | no |
| Listen publicly with no tokens (something in front signs people in) | `auth.insecure` | `--insecure` | `ATLAS_INSECURE` | no |
| The admin token (also `ATLAS_PUBLISH_TOKEN` and `ATLAS_READ_TOKEN` for the other roles, or `auth.tokens` in the file) | `auth.tokens` |  | `ATLAS_TOKEN` | none: the server is open and listens on this machine only |
| The configuration file | `(the file itself)` | `--config <file>` | `ATLAS_CONFIG` | `./atlas.server.json` when it exists |
| Largest uploaded object in MiB | `limits.maxObjectMiB` |  | `ATLAS_MAX_OBJECT_MIB` | `256` |
| Largest JSON upload in MiB | `limits.maxJsonMiB` |  | `ATLAS_MAX_JSON_MIB` | `32` |
| Maximum simultaneous live viewers | `limits.maxStreams` |  | `ATLAS_MAX_STREAMS` | `500` |
| Live connection heartbeat in seconds | `heartbeatSeconds` |  | `ATLAS_HEARTBEAT_SECONDS` | `15` |
| Live producer heartbeat timeout in seconds | `runTimeoutSeconds` |  | `ATLAS_RUN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `30` |
| Live run progress stall timeout in seconds (0 disables) | `runStallSeconds` |  | `ATLAS_RUN_STALL_SECONDS` | `900` |
| No request log | `log` | `--no-log` | `ATLAS_LOG` | one JSON line per request |
<!-- /generated:server-settings -->

`ATLAS_HOST` and `ATLAS_PORT` win over `HOST` and `PORT`, which other tools on a machine often set for their own
purposes.

## Storage

The server has one backend, the S3 bucket named by the [required variables](#required-s3-storage); it reads every
layer in it and shows one report. If the bucket becomes unreachable the server keeps serving what it has, names the
backend in the client and `/readyz`, and recovers by itself.

- **Uploads go to the bucket** and are in the report at once. Layers written to the bucket by something else (CI
  with bucket access, `atlas report merge`) are found at the next refresh.
- **Projects** are folders in the bucket (`projects/<slug>/`), as [below](#multiple-projects-on-one-node).
- **Clients are different.** `atlas report publish --store …` on a laptop or CI job may name any store (a folder,
  a bucket, this server's URL); this page is about the server.
- **Library use.** `createAtlasServer({ backends, write })` accepts any `ObjectStore` so an application embedding the
  server, or a test, can bring its own; `atlas serve` and `atlas dev` always use S3.

## Tokens and roles

| Role | May |
| --- | --- |
| `read` | look: the client, the report, `/api/status` |
| `publish` | also upload layers, specs and runs, and remove the scratch objects `atlas report doctor` writes |
| `admin` | all server operations |

Tokens are at least 12 characters (`openssl rand -hex 24`) and different from one another. Give them as
`ATLAS_TOKEN` (admin), `ATLAS_PUBLISH_TOKEN`, `ATLAS_READ_TOKEN`, or under `auth.tokens` in the file, preferably
with `tokenEnv` so the file holds no secret.

- **Sending a token:** `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. A browser's sign-in box also works for *looking* (any
  user name, the token as the password). **Uploading needs the Bearer header, never the sign-in box**: a browser
  sends those credentials by itself to any page that asks, which would let another site upload with them.
- **No tokens** means open, and then the server refuses to listen beyond this machine unless told
  `--insecure` (for when a proxy in front does the signing in).
- `/healthz` and `/readyz` never need a token, so a load balancer can use them.
- Only this server's own clients need tokens; Atlas does not do accounts. Put it behind what your company already
  uses (Cloudflare Access, an ALB with OIDC, `oauth2-proxy`, Tailscale) and TLS ends there too.

## Sending results

Every route ends as the same immutable layers, so use what fits:

| From | How |
| --- | --- |
| a CI job or laptop, after the run | `ATLAS_STORE=https://atlas.example.com ATLAS_TOKEN=… atlas report publish --producer unit --junit out.xml --specs ./specs` |
| a suite that can print JSON lines | `my-suite --json \| atlas report stream --producer e2e --environment ios` |
| code | `createReporter(identity, { store: httpStore({ url, token }) })`, below |
| anything that can make a request | `POST /api/checks` with a JSON body |
| a folder of layers you already have | `atlas report merge --store ./layers --into https://atlas.example.com` |

`ATLAS_STORE` may name the server instead of a folder or bucket: **every `atlas report` command works against it**
(`publish`, `stream`, `merge --into`, `doctor`, `status`). Keys never go in the URL; put the token in
`ATLAS_TOKEN` (or the first line of the file named by `ATLAS_TOKEN_FILE`). **A token belongs to one server.** With
one server in `ATLAS_STORE`, `ATLAS_TOKEN` is its token; with several, name each (`lab=https://lab.example.com`) and give
it `ATLAS_TOKEN_LAB`, because `ATLAS_TOKEN` is then sent to none of them. A token is never sent over plain `http://`
beyond this machine (`ATLAS_TRUST_NETWORK=1` says the network is yours).

### Streaming a run as it happens

`atlas report stream` reads one check per line (the fields of a check: `id`, `title`, `status`, and any
[evidence](extending.md)) and sends what has finished every second as a layer. A check sent first as `running` and
then as `passed` is two layers; the later, completed one wins, so the report follows the suite while it runs and
agrees with it when it ends. A layer that cannot be sent is kept and sent again, byte for byte the same, so a
retry never makes a second layer. It exits 1 if anything could not be sent.

```ts
import { createReporter } from '@crvouga/atlas/reports/reporter';
import { httpStore } from '@crvouga/atlas/reports/http-store';

const reporter = createReporter(
  { producer: 'web-e2e', environment: 'desktop-web', branch: process.env.GITHUB_REF_NAME ?? null },
  { store: httpStore({ url: 'https://atlas.example.com', token: process.env.ATLAS_TOKEN }), flushMs: 1000 }
);
reporter.check({ id: 'checkout > pays', title: 'pays', status: 'running', specPath: 'specs/checkout.feature' });
// …
reporter.check({ id: 'checkout > pays', title: 'pays', status: 'passed', specPath: 'specs/checkout.feature', attachments: [{ name: 'end.png', data: png }] });
const { layers, checks, lost } = await reporter.close();   // never throws into the suite; `lost` counts what never arrived
```

### `POST /api/checks`

```sh
curl -X POST https://atlas.example.com/api/checks -H "authorization: Bearer $ATLAS_TOKEN" -d '{
  "producer": "smoke", "environment": "prod",
  "checks": [{ "id": "login", "title": "can log in", "status": "passed" }]
}'
# 201 {"ok":true,"id":"…","checks":1}
```

The body is [the checks file](integrating.md) (`recordedAtMs` defaults to now). Binary evidence goes in as
`base64`. Anything wrong is a `422` that says what.

### The store protocol

`httpStore` is an `ObjectStore` over `/api/store`, so `publishChecks`, spec sets, run uploads and `copyStore` work
against a server unchanged. A client uploads **in dependency order**: blobs, then the manifest, then the catalog
entry that makes it visible. The server checks each step and says no to a catalog entry whose manifest is not
there (`409`), so nothing half-uploaded is ever shown.

## Tagging artifacts

A reviewer can mark a recording `#demo` after it was uploaded without uploading it again. The layer is immutable, so the
tag is kept beside it: each edit is one small object under `curation/artifact-tags/` in the write backend (or the live
store of a relay), named by time, never changed or removed. It records the attachment (layer, check, and the attachment's
`id`, else its bytes' key, else its name), the normalized tags added and removed, the name of the token that made the
edit, and the server's time. Nothing about the layer, its results or the report's winners changes.

- `GET /api/reports/artifact-tags` (read) returns every edit, oldest first. Fold them to get the tags that stand now: the
  last edit of a tag wins.
- `POST /api/reports/artifact-tags` (publish, `Authorization: Bearer`) records an edit. A read token, an anonymous reader
  and the browser's sign-in box are refused (`403`/`401`) like any upload, so a read-only visitor can see the tags and
  not change them. The viewer asks for a token when a reviewer adds a tag and keeps it only in that tab.
- Producer tags (`tags` on the attachment) and reviewer tags are kept apart everywhere: the viewer says who added a
  reviewer tag and when, and a reviewer can remove only reviewer tags. `capabilities.artifactTags` on `/api/server` says
  a server has this.

See [Tagging artifacts and demos](rich-evidence.md#tagging-artifacts-and-demos) for the tag rules. Reviewer tags are
shown in the viewer's evidence; the tests API (`artifactTag`) searches the producers' tags.

## Streaming

`GET /api/events` is a server-sent-events stream:

| Event | Data | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hello` | `{ version, ready, time, heartbeatMs? }` | Sent first. The report's current version. |
| `report` | `{ version, totalLayers, added: [{ id, producer, environment, branch, sha, recordedAtMs, counts }], addedTotal }` | Layers arrived. Enough to say who sent what, without asking. |
| `atlas:change` | `{ scope: "specs" \| "runs", files, runIds }` | New specs or runs. |
| `run` | A bounded `LiveRun` snapshot | Start, progress logs, heartbeat, completion, and interruption; no producer credentials. |
| `projects` | `{}` | Another project was discovered; refresh the project picker. |
| `ping` | `{}` | Every 15 s, so proxies keep the connection and the client can tell a quiet server from a dead connection. |

Run events update progress directly in the client cache. Report and specification events trigger coalesced reads of the affected data. Events arriving during a read cause a trailing refresh rather than cancelling that read. A client that missed some (a dropped
connection, a laptop that slept) loses nothing: it reads again when it reconnects, and the client also reads on a
slow timer behind the stream. Past `limits.maxStreams` viewers the server answers `503` with `Retry-After` and the
client polls instead; a client that stops reading is let go rather than held in memory.

### Reading only what changed

`GET /api/reports/evidence/effective` is the whole report: only the layers that win a check, each with only the
rows that win, with an ETag. A client that holds a version asks `?since=<version>` and is sent **only the layers
that changed since, and the ids that no longer win anything** (`"delta": true`). Applying that gives exactly the
report the server would have sent whole (`applyEffectiveDelta`, tested against every earlier version of random
runs); a version the server does not remember, or an older server, answers with the whole report, which a client
takes as it always did. A result streamed into a 100 000-check report costs a client a few kilobytes.

## Reading the report as an agent

The effective report says what each check's result is now. To explore a project, or to answer "what is tested,
where, how long does it take, what is flaky", read the tests instead. Every endpoint here answers JSON, or Markdown
with `format=markdown` (or `Accept: text/markdown`), and takes the project prefix like every other
(`/api/projects/<slug>/reports/tests`).

| Ask | Endpoint |
| --- | --- |
| Every test, a summary (by status, environment, producer, domain), insights (failing, flaky, slowest) and facets | `GET /api/reports/tests` |
| Only some: `q` (all words), `status` (or `flaky`), `environment`, `producer`, `domain`, `spec`, `tag`, `run`; `sort`, `offset`, `limit` | `GET /api/reports/tests?status=failed&environment=ios` |
| One test: every recorded result (status, duration, environment, branch, commit, CI run), newest first | `GET /api/reports/tests/history?key=<key>` |
| Why Specs, domains and counts disagree: ambiguous spec paths, shared domains, gaps, a reconciliation of the totals | `GET /api/reports/tests/health` |
| The runs that recorded the report (by CI run URL, else branch and commit); `?video=true` keeps those with a playable video | `GET /api/reports/runs` |
| Every test one run recorded | `GET /api/reports/runs/detail?key=<run key>` |

```sh
curl "$ATLAS_SERVER_URL/api/projects/$ATLAS_PROJECT/reports/tests?format=markdown&limit=50"
```

- A **test** is a check identity, its spec path and id, across producers and environments. `outcomes` holds its
  current result on each environment (the report's winners, so a test's status here is always the gate's);
  `stats` describes its recorded history: pass rate, flips, whether it is flaky and why (it passed and failed on the
  same commit, passed only after a retry, or its producer said so), durations (avg, p50, p95, min, max, last), runs
  and branches.
- The **health** document explains the numbers instead of adding one. It keeps spec files, defined specs, specs with an
  executed test, tests, outlines, examples and per-environment observations apart, and walks from the Specs total to
  the Tests total. Two spec paths are one logical spec only when a mapping says so
  (`?root=<from>><to>`, for example `?root=%3Especs/` to put `checkout/cart.feature` under `specs/`); similar paths
  are reported as ambiguous and never merged, and a similar title is never an identity. Give a check the label
  `outline` to say which scenario outline an example belongs to. A domain shared by nearly every spec is flagged, but
  explicit domain metadata always stays authoritative. The document only reads: it changes no status.
- The server keeps the newest 100 results of every test (progress reported as `running` is not history) and every run's last result per test, in memory, as layers
  arrive; it is rebuilt from the layers on restart. History never changes a result.
- Without a published spec set, tests are grouped under the specs their layers recorded (`specs[]`: path, domain,
  title), and the gate and the outline do the same, so a project needs no spec set to be browsable. A path no layer
  described is titled from its file name and grouped by its folder under `specs/`.
- Statistics are only as rich as what producers send: durations need `durationMs`, devices need an environment and
  labels (`browser`, `device`, `os`), videos and screenshots need attachments. See
  [Send rich evidence](rich-evidence.md).

Every operation, parameter, body, response and error is in [the HTTP API reference](reference/http-api.md) and, for tools, in `openapi.json`.
<!-- /generated:server-operations -->

Errors are always [RFC 9457](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457) problem documents (`application/problem+json`: `type`,
`title`, `status`, and a `detail` that says what to do; `error` repeats `detail` for older clients) with a status that says
what to do: `401` send a token, `403` that token may not, `409` upload what this depends on first or you are changing
something immutable, `413` too large, `422` not valid, `503` still starting (see `Retry-After`).

**For agents:** a server describes itself. `GET /api/openapi.json` is the OpenAPI 3.1 description of everything above (also
shipped as `@crvouga/atlas/openapi.json`) and `GET /llms.txt` is a guide for an agent that was handed only the server's address;
neither needs a token. See [Atlas for AI agents](agents.md).

## What the server refuses

What is checked is what would otherwise corrupt the report for everyone, and it is checked from the bytes in hand:

- **Everything is named by its content.** A manifest whose content does not hash to its id (it was edited, or written
  by something that does not follow the format) is refused, as is one that is not a valid layer; so is a blob
  (the digest of what is in it) or a spec file that is not what its name says.
- **Dependencies come first.** A manifest needs its blobs; a catalog entry needs its manifest; a spec set needs its
  files; a run's catalog entry needs its manifest.
- **Layers are immutable.** The same bytes again are fine (a retry); other bytes under the same key are a `409`.
- **A run that did not pass its privacy scan is never shared.**
- **Only keys Atlas writes**, under `layers/`, without traversal, backslashes or control characters.
- **Size.** Bodies over `limits.maxObjectMiB` are refused as they arrive, not after they were held.
- **Attachment bytes are untrusted.** They are served only through one function that forces a safe type and a
  sandbox, whatever the producer claimed.

## Performance

`bun packages/server/bench/bench.ts [layers] [checks]` seeds a long history and measures the server on it. On a
laptop with 2 000 layers of 100 checks (200 000 results, 10 000 slots) and with 1 000 layers of 1 000 checks
(100 000 slots, a 22 MB report):

| | 10 000 slots | 100 000 slots |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start: read and fold every layer | 0.4 s | 1.7 s |
| A refresh with nothing new | 4 ms | 4 ms |
| Upload one layer → every client told | 4 ms | 5 ms |
| `GET effective`, cached / `304` | 1 ms / 0.2 ms | 13 ms / 0.5 ms |
| `GET status`, cached for the version | 12 ms first | 70 ms first |

What makes it so, none of it at the cost of the contract:

- **A layer is read once.** The report is folded incrementally; only layers that still hold a winner are kept, so
  memory follows the number of checks and not the age of the project.
- **A change costs one layer.** Each layer remembers the JSON of what it sends, the version is a hash of per-layer
  digests, and a delta lists only layers that changed, so the work to take in a result does not grow with the
  report.
- **An upload is read once.** A layer's manifest is parsed and verified when it arrives and handed to the report,
  not read again; blob existence is asked 16 at a time.
- **The newest end of the catalog is all a refresh looks at**, with a full look now and then.
- **Compressed once.** The client's files are brotli-compressed once (gzip for clients that cannot read it), a
  report version is gzipped once however many viewers fetch it, and events are encoded once for every client.
- **A small client.** The graph, the Gherkin parser, the recording player and the finder load when used: the
  first page is about 250 KB over the wire.

## Operating it

- **One node for multiple projects.** Local environments and CI select their project slug and talk to the same node, which tells
  every client at once. Two servers on one backend both work and show the same report, but a client hears about
  an upload only from the server that took it and about the other's at the next refresh, so give a team one.
- **State is the bucket.** Reports and user state are all in it. Back it up, replicate or version it as any data;
  starting a new server on a restored copy shows the same report and applies the same garbage collection policy.
- **Stopping.** `SIGTERM` stops accepting, lets requests in flight finish, ends the event streams and exits 0.
- **Logs.** One JSON line per request (method, path, status, ms) to stdout, none for the probes. The first lines
  say which bucket it uses, what the garbage collection policy in S3 is (or that none is saved), and warn when there are no tokens.
- **A backend goes down.** The server keeps serving what it has, names the backend in the client and in
  `/readyz`, and recovers by itself. The gate fails closed: unknown is not a pass.
- **Upgrades.** The layer format is a stable, versioned contract; upgrade the server before the clients that
  publish when a release says the format moved.

## Configure from the client

Open **Settings** (`/admin`) and enter an admin token. The token stays in page memory. Read and publish tokens cannot edit settings; the browser sign-in box only grants reading. The API uses `Authorization: Bearer` and refuses cross-origin browser writes.

The page has a Storage notice (the bucket is set by the `ATLAS_S3_*` variables and cannot be changed here), the **Garbage collection** form, and the Live updates and Report rules forms. Advanced includes request limits, logging, a JSON editor, and a read-only view of the active configuration.

- **Garbage collection** edits the policy: enabled, delete layers older than N days, always keep the newest N layers, run every N hours. *Save garbage collection policy* writes it to S3 at once (it applies at the next pass, no restart). *Preview deletions* counts what a pass would delete, per project, and deletes nothing. See [user state and garbage collection](#user-state-and-garbage-collection).
- **Settings** forms save to the same JSON document in S3 and apply after a restart. Atlas validates them against the whole deployment first, and the configuration file, environment variables and flags retain precedence. Concurrent edits require reloading the current revision. Data is never moved or removed by changing settings. Embedded servers can provide their own persistence or manage settings outside this API.

Native test reporters for CodeceptJS, Mocha, Jest and Node upload directly to this server; see [runner setup](runners.md). Every publisher uses the same server address and only a publish token. Storage credentials belong in the server environment.

## Live test runs and heartbeats

The default native reporters and statechart runner stream tests and steps through `/api/live`, before the invocation finishes. Running tests appear inside their report with an animated status mark and the latest step. Open a test to read its progress log; its previous recorded result stays available separately. The **Running** filter narrows both the spec list and the test rows, and counts update as tests finish or time out. Statechart tests appear inside the chart and screen details. Selecting an archived run leaves live progress out of that historical view. Finished checks immediately enter normal immutable report layers. Operational progress is separate from historical winners, so a previous passed result never implies that the current invocation passed.

Start with `POST /api/live/<uuid>`, send ordered check deltas with `PATCH /api/live/<uuid>`, and renew the producer lease with `POST /api/live/<uuid>/heartbeat` every 5 seconds. Finish with a terminal update. Only the publisher token that registered the invocation can update it. Replayed sequences must have identical content; late writes cannot revive an expired invocation. `createLiveReporter` handles batching, retries, heartbeat timers and the final flush.

The server uses its own receipt clock. By default it interrupts a run after 30 seconds without a heartbeat (`ATLAS_RUN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`). Heartbeats do not reset progress: after 15 minutes with no changed tests/steps, a separate stall timeout interrupts it (`ATLAS_RUN_STALL_SECONDS`, 0 disables). Both settings are editable in the admin UI. Healthy long tests continue renewing heartbeats; increase or disable the progress timeout for tests that legitimately make no observable progress for longer.

Interrupted runs retain completed results and show why the remaining work stopped. Missing outcomes never become passes. The server persists bounded summaries under `server/live/` in its bucket and restores outstanding leases as interrupted after a server restart. S3 server credentials need GetObject/PutObject for that prefix; generate the updated `atlas report policy --role both` policy. Producers still receive no backend credentials. Live `run` events carry bounded snapshots directly into test rows, including step logs and interruption reasons. The legacy `atlas:change` announcement remains available for older clients; its optional `liveRunId` identifies lease updates. Reconnecting viewers re-fetch progress, reports, and specifications. With SSE connected, live progress uses a 60-second safety refresh; without SSE it polls every two seconds. Returning to the tab or coming back online also revalidates reports and progress.

In this repository, use `bun atlas` and `bun example:run` in two terminals. Every example Gherkin scenario executes, including sharing and renaming; `@unrecorded` no longer excludes tests.

## Multiple projects on one node

Start the node with `atlas server` (or `bun atlas` in this repository). The server builds or finds the Atlas client and serves it with the API from one process. It never imports a consumer or an example. In this repository the node uses port 5180 and the bucket named by your `.env`; `bun example:run` publishes the Todo app to project `todo-app`.

Set `ATLAS_PROJECT=todo-app` alongside `ATLAS_SERVER_URL` for native reporters and statechart runs. Report CLI commands accept `--project todo-app` (or `ATLAS_PROJECT`) with an HTTP store. Programmatic HTTP stores, live reporters and native reporter options accept `project: 'todo-app'`. Keep the same slug for the invocation's live progress, final results, spec sets and recordings. Slugs use 1–64 lowercase letters, digits or hyphens, starting and ending with a letter or digit.

Every project API is available as `/api/projects/<slug>/…`, for example `/api/projects/todo-app/checks`, `/api/projects/todo-app/events` and `/api/projects/todo-app/reports/evidence/effective`. The unprefixed API accepts optional `?project=todo-app` or `X-Atlas-Project: todo-app`. Conflicting selectors are refused. `GET /api/projects` discovers projects. A successful authenticated upload creates a project; reads of an unknown project return 404.

Projects isolate check identities, specs, run IDs, recordings, lease summaries, event streams and report caches. Identical layer bytes are preserved as uploaded. The node stores each project's objects under `projects/<slug>/` and discovery markers under `server/projects/`. Unqualified requests continue reading the legacy default namespace, advertised as **Default** when it has reports. Existing data is never implicitly moved. For S3, use the combined server policy (`atlas report policy --role both`) with access to both project namespaces and the catalog. An HTTP relay selects the same project on its upstream node and keeps discovery and leases locally.

The project picker sits at the top right; the header also provides spec dropdown breadcrumbs. Project selection lives in the page URL, so links and refreshes preserve it. Switching projects reloads the client, clearing report queries, media and event connections. Custom report-source preferences are keyed by the project's data URL. Project namespaces share the node's authentication roles: they are organizational partitions, not separate tenant authorization policies. Settings and server identity remain node-wide.

Project indexes are opened lazily; at most 64 are active in memory. An index with no active requests or event subscribers is closed after five idle minutes. Event subscribers share the node-wide stream limit. Project discovery lists only small catalog markers, never every report layer.
</doc>

<doc path="docs/deploying.md">
# Running Atlas for a project: one server

This is the production setup. A project runs **one Atlas server**. Developers' machines and every CI job send
their results to it, as they finish or when they are done, and it shows everyone, developers and the business
alike, the whole project at once, live. It keeps results (and all its user state) in an S3-compatible bucket and
nowhere else; nothing is partitioned by run, branch or person: results are layered. The server's API,
configuration and protocol are in **[the Atlas server](server.md)**; this page is the path to production.

```
  a developer's worktree ─┐                                       ┌─▶ developers   (browser, live)
  a CI job, any branch ───┼─ atlas report publish|stream ─▶ SERVER ◀┤   atlas serve: keeps layers in S3
  a device lab, nightly ──┘   (immutable layers, over HTTP)  ──▶ S3  ├─▶ business      (required, nothing else)
                                                                    └─▶ CI gate     atlas report status
```

Why this holds together:

- **Publishing never conflicts.** A layer is one immutable file named by its content. Two machines that
  publish at once write different files; a retry writes the same one. There is no lock, no index to
  corrupt, nothing to merge.
- **The server is replaceable.** What it knows is in its bucket. Replace it, restore it
  from a backup, or run a copy on a laptop: they show the same report, because a report is a function of the
  layers ([the contract](report-contract.md)).
- **One view.** The newest completed result of every check, in every environment, from anyone. A
  developer's local run on a feature branch, CI on `main` and a device lab's nightly sit side by side.
  Narrow it only when you choose to ([filters](#5-choosing-what-takes-part)).

- [1. Where results are kept](#1-where-results-are-kept)
- [2. Check it](#2-check-it)
- [3. Send results from CI and from laptops](#3-send-results-from-ci-and-from-laptops)
- [4. The server](#4-the-server)
- [5. Choosing what takes part](#5-choosing-what-takes-part)
- [6. Operating it](#6-operating-it)
- [7. Performance](#7-performance)
- [8. Troubleshooting](#8-troubleshooting)

## 1. Where results are kept

**The server keeps everything in one S3-compatible bucket** (reports and user state, such as the garbage collection
policy), set by the required `ATLAS_S3_ENDPOINT`, `ATLAS_S3_BUCKET`, `ATLAS_S3_REGION`, `ATLAS_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and
`ATLAS_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` variables ([details](server.md#required-s3-storage), template in
[`.env.example`](https://github.com/crvouga/atlas/blob/main/.env.example)). Without them it refuses to start, listing
every variable and what is wrong. There is no disk or database to fall back to, so the server is replaceable:
a new one started on the same bucket shows the same report.

**Clients and CI** name stores by URL, and a client may publish straight to a bucket or folder as well as to the
server. A store is named by a URL. Keys never go in it.

| Store | URL |
| --- | --- |
| AWS S3 | `s3://my-bucket/atlas/my-project` (add `?region=eu-west-1` if `AWS_REGION` is not set) |
| A folder | `/srv/atlas`, `./atlas-reports` (a CI workspace, an NFS mount, a laptop) |
| Cloudflare R2 | `r2://bucket/atlas/my-project?account=<account id>` (or `R2_ACCOUNT_ID`), with the R2 token's keys in `ATLAS_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID` / `ATLAS_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` |
| Google Cloud Storage | `gs://bucket/atlas/my-project`, with an HMAC key pair in `ATLAS_S3_*` |
| MinIO, Backblaze B2, Wasabi, SeaweedFS, any S3-compatible | `s3://bucket/atlas/my-project?endpoint=https://host&region=auto` |

Atlas talks to S3 itself, signing requests with Signature Version 4 and sending them with `fetch`: no
SDK, no extra install, the same on Bun and Node. It is tested against AWS's published signing vectors
and, for real, against a live S3 server (SeaweedFS) in CI. Stores other than AWS and SeaweedFS speak the
same protocol; the `r2://` and `gs://` shorthands only fill in the endpoint. None of them is part of Atlas's own tests,
so run `atlas report doctor` against yours before relying on it.

**On AWS:**

1. Create a bucket. Keep "block all public access" on. Default encryption (SSE-S3) needs nothing more; with
   SSE-KMS the roles below also need `kms:Decrypt` and `kms:GenerateDataKey` on the key.
2. Use one folder per project (`atlas/my-project/`). Several projects can share a bucket.
3. Create two roles. `atlas report policy` prints each, scoped to the bucket and folder:

   ```sh
   atlas report policy --store s3://my-bucket/atlas/my-project --role publisher   # CI and developers
   atlas report policy --store s3://my-bucket/atlas/my-project --role reader      # a server that only reads it, and the gate
   # the server that uploads into it needs --role both (also grants server/live/* for live leases)
   ```

   A publisher may write and read `layers/*` and list the folder. A reader may read `layers/*` and list.
   Nobody needs to delete or overwrite: **do not grant it**. (`s3:ListBucket` is for publishers too: without
   it S3 answers "403 forbidden" instead of "404 not found" when asked whether a layer exists yet.)
4. Do not put a lifecycle rule that expires `layers/`. Old layers are cheap and are history. If storage
   grows, expire `layers/runs/` (screenshots and clips) first.

Versioning and replication are optional: nothing is ever overwritten with different bytes.

## 2. Check it

```sh
export ATLAS_STORE=s3://my-bucket/atlas/my-project
atlas report doctor                    # a role that can do everything
atlas report doctor --role publisher   # what CI and developers can do
atlas report doctor --role reader      # what a reader can do
```

```
my-project
  ✓ store     s3://my-bucket/atlas/my-project/ (us-east-1)
  ✓ list      38 ms, credentials from AWS CLI (profile default)
  ✓ contents  1240 layers (newest 2026-10-09T11:59:00.000Z), 3 spec sets, 12 runs
  ✓ write     wrote, listed, read back and deleted a scratch object: the store meets the ObjectStore contract
All good.
```

Each failure says what to fix: the permission that is missing, the region that is wrong, the clock that is
off. The credentials come from the same places an AWS SDK looks, in this order: `ATLAS_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID` /
`ATLAS_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` (so one store can use keys that are not the machine's AWS keys), then
`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` / `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, EKS web identity (IRSA), ECS task roles,
`~/.aws/credentials`, the AWS CLI (which covers SSO, assumed roles and `credential_process`), and EC2
instance metadata. Credentials that expire are refreshed before they do.

## 3. Send results from CI and from laptops

Every environment runs the same command. Set `ATLAS_STORE` once and it needs no flags for the store.

### To the server

```sh
export ATLAS_STORE=https://atlas.example.com     # once, in .envrc, CI variables or your shell profile
export ATLAS_TOKEN=…                             # a publish token of the server (never in the URL)
bun test --reporter=junit --reporter-outfile=out.xml
bunx atlas report publish --producer unit --junit out.xml --specs ./specs --environment desktop-web
```

The result is in everyone's view within a few milliseconds, with no bucket credentials anywhere, and no
artifacts to merge. To show a long suite *while it runs*, stream it: `my-suite --json | atlas report stream
--producer e2e --environment ios` ([sending results](server.md#sending-results)). The gate asks the server for the
verdict, so only the verdict travels: `atlas report status --branch main --ignore-modified`.
[`examples/deploy/github-actions.yml`](https://github.com/crvouga/atlas/blob/main/examples/deploy/github-actions.yml)
is the whole workflow, publishers and gate. The rest of this section is publishing straight to a bucket, for
CI that has bucket access and no route to the server.

### Straight to the bucket

### CI

Give CI a role, not a key. On GitHub Actions that is OIDC, so no AWS secret is stored anywhere. Every
node publishes its own layers straight to the bucket: no artifacts to download and merge. The server finds them
at its next refresh.

```yaml
permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read }
env: { ATLAS_STORE: "s3://my-bucket/atlas/my-project" }
steps:
  - run: bun test --reporter=junit --reporter-outfile=out.xml
    continue-on-error: true            # a failing suite must still publish: a failure is evidence
  - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
    with: { role-to-assume: "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/atlas-publisher", aws-region: us-east-1 }
  - run: bunx atlas report publish --producer unit --junit out.xml --specs ./specs --environment desktop-web
    if: always()
```

`--sha`, `--branch` and the run URL come from the CI's variables. `--specs ./specs` also publishes the
specs themselves, so the server can show them without a checkout (below).

### A developer's laptop

```sh
aws sso login                                    # or any way you sign in to AWS
export ATLAS_STORE=s3://my-bucket/atlas/my-project   # once, in .envrc or your shell profile
bun test --reporter=junit --reporter-outfile=out.xml
bunx atlas report publish --producer unit --junit out.xml --specs ./specs --environment desktop-web
```

Atlas sees from git whether the worktree has uncommitted edits to tracked files. If it does, the layer is
marked **modified**: it appears in the shared view with the warning "Potentially outdated: recorded from a
modified checkout", never as the commit's own result. Outside a git checkout the origin is **unknown**.
A CI checkout is the commit it names. Untracked files (build output, `out.xml`) do not count.

Through the server a result is in the shared view at once; straight to a bucket, within the server's refresh interval
(10 seconds by default).

### What lands in the bucket

| Key | What | Written by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `layers/manifests/<id>.json`, `layers/index/…` | One layer of checks, and its catalog entry | `publish` |
| `layers/specs/blobs/<sha256>.txt`, `layers/specs/sets/<id>.json`, `layers/specs/index/…` | The specs of one commit, by content | `publish --specs` |
| `layers/runs/<run>/…`, `layers/runs/index/…` | A statechart run with its screenshots and clips | `publish --manifest … --upload-run` |

Everything is immutable and addressed by its content, so each publish is safe to repeat and safe to run
in parallel. A set of specs is named by the files and the commit, so publishing the same commit from ten
nodes writes it once.

For statecharts, publish each run as a layer and upload it for the client:

```sh
bunx atlas run --config atlas.config.ts --shard 1/2
bunx atlas report publish --producer statecharts --environment desktop-web \
  --manifest atlas-runs/<run>/manifest.json --specs ./specs --upload-run
```

A run is uploaded only when its privacy scan passed: the same rule the static client applies.

## 4. The server

```sh
atlas serve                    # ATLAS_S3_* says where; listens on :8080
```

It serves the client, the report and the project's specs and runs from its bucket. It also
accepts uploads and announces new results on its event stream. The bucket's credentials need list, read, write and delete
permissions (`atlas report policy` prints a least-privilege policy; delete is for the garbage collection you define in the UI).

| Flag | Environment | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| | `ATLAS_S3_ENDPOINT`, `ATLAS_S3_BUCKET`, `ATLAS_S3_REGION`, `ATLAS_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `ATLAS_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` | **Required.** The S3-compatible bucket that holds all reports and user state. Optional: `ATLAS_S3_PREFIX`, `ATLAS_S3_PATH_STYLE`, `ATLAS_S3_SESSION_TOKEN`. |
| `--port <n>` | `ATLAS_PORT` or `PORT` | Default 8080. `0` picks a free one. |
| `--host <h>` | `ATLAS_HOST` or `HOST` | Default `127.0.0.1`. Listening beyond this machine requires tokens or `--insecure`. |
| `--site <dir>` | `ATLAS_SITE` | The built client. Default: `./atlas-site`, else built once into `~/.cache/atlas/site`. |
| `--outline-branch <b>` | `ATLAS_OUTLINE_BRANCH` | Which branch's specs the report is laid over. Default `main`, then `master`, then the newest. |
| `--refresh <seconds>` | `ATLAS_REFRESH_SECONDS` | How often the bucket is looked at for new layers. Default 10. |
| `--branch <name>` (repeatable) | `ATLAS_ONLY_BRANCH` | Only layers recorded on these branches take part. |
| `--ignore-modified` | `ATLAS_IGNORE_MODIFIED=1` | Leave out layers from modified checkouts and unknown origins. |
| | `ATLAS_TOKEN`, `ATLAS_PUBLISH_TOKEN`, `ATLAS_READ_TOKEN` | Admin, publisher and reader tokens, each at least 12 characters. Send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, or HTTP Basic with the token as the password. Probes require no token. |

### Run it

**Railway (deploy an image, no repository or code changes).** Create a service from the Docker image
`ghcr.io/crvouga/atlas:latest`. Copy the URI below into Railway's image field:

```text
ghcr.io/crvouga/atlas:latest
```

For a specific revision, open a [CI run](https://github.com/crvouga/atlas/actions/workflows/ci.yml)'s
**Summary → Atlas CI**: it includes the published commit image URI, immutable digest and whether that run
updated `latest`. Pull request builds and failed publications are labelled accordingly.

1. In Railway choose **New service → Docker image** and enter `ghcr.io/crvouga/atlas:latest`.
   Leave the start command unset: the image includes the server and the prebuilt viewer.
2. Add `ATLAS_TOKEN` with a long random value (generate one with `openssl rand -hex 24`). It grants admin
   access; optionally add separate `ATLAS_PUBLISH_TOKEN` and `ATLAS_READ_TOKEN` for publishers and readers.
3. Add the five required storage variables (`ATLAS_S3_ENDPOINT`, `ATLAS_S3_BUCKET`, `ATLAS_S3_REGION`,
   `ATLAS_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `ATLAS_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`) for a bucket you own. The service keeps nothing on its own
   disk, so no volume is needed and a replaced image loses nothing; without the variables it exits and lists each one.
   Keep one replica.
4. Set the healthcheck path to `/readyz` and generate a public domain. The image listens on `0.0.0.0` and
   honors Railway's `PORT`; leave `ATLAS_PORT` unset. Open the domain and sign in with your token as the
   password (any username), or use the viewer's token sign-in.
5. Under **Settings → Source → Configure Auto Updates**, enable image updates and select **Anytime**.
   Each successful `main` build publishes a new `latest`. Railway detects the changed digest and redeploys
   within its update schedule; detection can be cached for a few hours, so publishing does not mean an
   immediate deployment ([Railway image auto updates](https://docs.railway.com/deployments/image-auto-updates)).

Check the domain with `curl --fail https://YOUR-DOMAIN/readyz`: HTTP 200 means the server read its backend.
Projects publish to that domain with `ATLAS_STORE=https://YOUR-DOMAIN` and their `ATLAS_TOKEN`, as in
[sending results](#3-send-results-from-ci-and-from-laptops). Hosting Atlas needs no project checkout; publishing
your project's test results still needs the integration described there.

Then open `/admin` to define the garbage collection policy; until you save one, nothing is deleted.

### Deploy without authentication

Use `ghcr.io/crvouga/atlas-insecure:latest` for a server that requires no sign-in or API token. It is built
from the same commit, server and viewer as `ghcr.io/crvouga/atlas:latest`, with `ATLAS_INSECURE=true`
to allow listening on the network without tokens. Anonymous callers have full read, publish and admin access.
Anyone who discovers an unlisted URL can read reports, upload results and change settings; the URL is
not access control.

In Railway, create a **Docker image** service with:

```text
ghcr.io/crvouga/atlas-insecure:latest
```

Leave the start command unset. Add the required `ATLAS_S3_*` storage variables, keep one
replica, set the healthcheck to `/readyz` and generate a public domain. Leave `ATLAS_PORT` unset so Railway's
`PORT` is used. Enable **Settings → Source → Configure Auto Updates → Anytime** to follow `latest`.
Do not set `ATLAS_TOKEN`, `ATLAS_PUBLISH_TOKEN` or `ATLAS_READ_TOKEN`, or add `auth.tokens` to
a configuration file: configured tokens still enable authentication. Open the domain directly, including `/admin`
for settings (leave the token field blank and choose **Load settings**).

Verify anonymous reads and uploads without an Authorization header:

```sh
curl --fail https://YOUR-DOMAIN/readyz
curl --fail https://YOUR-DOMAIN/api/server
curl --fail 'https://YOUR-DOMAIN/api/checks?project=my-project' \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"producer":"smoke","checks":[{"id":"deployed","title":"Deployed","status":"passed"}]}'
```

Readiness returns HTTP 200, `/api/server` reports `"open":true` and `"role":"admin"`, and the upload returns
HTTP 201. Configure a project with `ATLAS_STORE=https://YOUR-DOMAIN` and `ATLAS_PROJECT=my-project`;
leave its `ATLAS_TOKEN` unset. Use the same publishing commands described in
[sending results](#3-send-results-from-ci-and-from-laptops), omitting credentials.

For local Docker:

```sh
docker run --pull always -p 8080:8080 --env-file .env ghcr.io/crvouga/atlas-insecure:latest
```

Both images publish full commit tags for pinning or rollback. A new GHCR package must be made Public
once before Railway can pull without registry credentials; see
[image publication](https://github.com/crvouga/atlas/blob/main/docs/releasing.md#server-image).

### Docker

The same published image works anywhere Docker runs. It already contains the client (the same
for every project: the server tells the page where its data is), and keeps nothing on its own disk: it needs the
`ATLAS_S3_*` variables (copy `.env.example` to `.env` and fill it in):

```sh
docker run --pull always -p 8080:8080 --env-file .env \
  -e ATLAS_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 24) ghcr.io/crvouga/atlas:latest
```

The image is built from each checked commit, independently of npm releases. To pin a deployment or roll
back, replace `latest` with the full commit SHA. To build from this repository, use `docker build -t atlas .`;
[`examples/deploy/Dockerfile`](https://github.com/crvouga/atlas/blob/main/examples/deploy/Dockerfile) is the
alternative for building from an npm version or a local package tarball.

The bucket's account needs the combined **both** policy (including `server/live/*` for producer leases and `server/state.json`
for user state) plus `s3:DeleteObject` for garbage collection. The server does not use ambient AWS roles: pass the keys.

**Try it on one machine.** [`examples/deploy/compose.yaml`](https://github.com/crvouga/atlas/blob/main/examples/deploy/compose.yaml)
starts the published image with an S3 server (SeaweedFS) and a bucket as its storage; `compose.s3.yaml` is the same stack without tokens.
Publish to `http://localhost:8080` from your project and open it.

**Kubernetes.** [`examples/deploy/kubernetes.yaml`](https://github.com/crvouga/atlas/blob/main/examples/deploy/kubernetes.yaml):
one copy (the server is a singleton for the project), results in the bucket (keys from a Secret), readiness on `/readyz`.

**Without a container.** `bun add -d @crvouga/atlas`, then `bunx atlas client build --no-data --out
atlas-site` and `bunx atlas serve`. Everything it can be told is in
[the Atlas server](server.md#configuration).

<!-- generated:runtime-requirements -->
Supported runtimes (from `package.json`): **node `>=22.18.0`** or **bun `>=1.2.0`**. Node consumers do not need Bun unless they use the Bun WebView driver.
<!-- /generated:runtime-requirements -->

### Who may look

Set `ATLAS_READ_TOKEN` for a dashboard that only accepts readers. `ATLAS_PUBLISH_TOKEN` also allows
uploads, and `ATLAS_TOKEN` grants administration. Without tokens the server listens on loopback by default. Put it behind what your
company already uses: an ALB with OIDC, Cloudflare Access, `oauth2-proxy`, Tailscale. TLS ends at that
layer too. Pass `--insecure` only when that proxy handles sign-in.

### What it serves

| Path | |
| --- | --- |
| `/` | The client. Its page carries the server's address book, so one build serves every project. |
| `/api/reports/evidence/effective` | The whole report in one request: only the layers that win a check, each with only the rows that win. ETag, gzip. |
| `/api/reports/evidence`, `/evidence/rows/<backend>/<id>`, `/outline`, `/outline/spec?path=` | History, one layer's checks, the specs. |
| `/api/reports/evidence/detail/<backend>/<id>?check=<id>&kind=<kind>` | Everything one result carries: its timeline, annotations, retries, attachments and extensions, and the run's own. Without `check`, only the run's. |
| `/api/reports/layers/<id>/blobs/<key>` | One file a layer carries (screenshot, video, trace…), served as untrusted bytes with range support, cached for good. |
| `/api/data/specs/…`, `/api/data/runs/…`, `/api/data/sources.json` | The specs and runs, laid out the way the client reads a static host. |
| `/api/checks` | Upload a layer of checks with `POST`. |
| `/api/events` | Live report updates over server-sent events. |
| `/healthz` | The process is up. |
| `/readyz` | `200` once the bucket was read and at least one store answers; `503` otherwise. Route traffic on this. |

The specs come from the newest **spec set** published from `main` (`publish --specs`), so the server needs no
checkout and no git access. A set from someone's modified worktree is used only if no committed one exists.

## 5. Choosing what takes part

By default every layer takes part: a report is the newest completed result of each check in each
environment, from wherever it was recorded. That is the unified view, and it is honest: a developer's run
on `feat/pay` shows up, labelled, until something newer replaces it.

Narrow it by choice, per consumer, never by moving data:

| You want | Use |
| --- | --- |
| A release gate that no laptop can turn red | `atlas report status --branch main --ignore-modified` |
| A pull request's gate that inherits what it did not re-run from `main` | `--branch "$PR_BRANCH" --branch main --ignore-modified` |
| A business dashboard of what is committed | `atlas serve --ignore-modified` |
| Everything, as the team lives it | nothing (the default) |
| One person's view of what leaving a source out changes | **Sources** in the client: leave out a branch, environment, version or layer |

## 6. Operating it

- **Upgrades.** The layer format is a stable, versioned contract. A server reads every layer a publisher of
  an older or the same schema version wrote, and names (never guesses at) a layer of a newer one. Upgrade
  readers (the server, the gate) before publishers when a release bumps `schemaVersion`; within a version
  they never need to move together.
- **Logs.** One JSON line per request to stdout. `/healthz` and `/readyz` are not logged. At start it
  prints what it reads and any store it cannot reach.
- **A store goes down.** The server keeps serving what it has, names the store in the client's notices and
  in `/readyz`, and recovers by itself. The gate fails closed: unknown is not a pass.
- **A layer cannot be read** (corrupt, or written by a newer Atlas): a notice names it. It is tried again
  every five minutes.
- **Scaling.** One Atlas node supports multiple project namespaces with independently loaded report indexes. It takes in an upload in milliseconds and a
  report of 100,000 checks costs a client kilobytes per change ([performance](server.md#performance)). Memory
  grows with the number of distinct checks, plus about a hundred bytes for each layer ever seen (to know it has
  read it). More than one server on a backend works and shows the same report, but each hears of uploads to
  another only at its next refresh.
- **Cost.** Between full listings a refresh asks for one page of the catalog, newest first, and stops at the
  first page it already knows: one `LIST` request every refresh interval, however long the history. A full
  listing (one request per thousand layers) runs at the start and every 30 refreshes (five minutes by
  default), which is also how a layer recorded with an old timestamp is found. One small `GET` per new
  layer, once.
- **Retention.** Atlas deletes nothing until you define a garbage collection policy in the UI (`/admin`); it is kept in the bucket as JSON and
  then removes only superseded layers older than you allow ([details](server.md#user-state-and-garbage-collection)). `atlas report doctor` shows what the bucket holds.
- **Disaster recovery.** The bucket is the only state (reports and user state). Back it up, replicate or version it as you
  do any data; a server is rebuilt from nothing in the time it takes to read the layers (below). It listens at once
  and answers `/readyz` 503 until it has, so a liveness probe never kills one that is still reading.
- **A second bucket.** The server reads one bucket. To combine another team's layers or an archive into the
  report, copy them in with `atlas report merge --into <store>`; clients and `atlas report status` may read several stores.

## 7. Performance

Measured, not promised (a laptop, a local S3 server, so these are the client's own costs; real S3 adds its
latency per request, which the server hides by reading 64 at a time):

| What | Cost |
| --- | --- |
| Publish a layer of plain checks | One `HEAD` and two small `PUT`s. Two thousand layers published in under two seconds from one process, in parallel. |
| Server start | About 0.2 ms of CPU per layer, plus S3 latency ÷ 64 per layer: 2,000 layers in well under a second on a fast store, a few seconds on S3. Each layer is read once, ever. |
| Refresh with nothing new | One `LIST` request for the newest page of the catalog, whatever the history. |
| The report, to a client | One request. 12,000 checks from 2,000 layers is 108 KB gzipped, built once per change. |
| The client asking again | `304 Not Modified` in under a millisecond. While the live stream is open it asks only when told, and then for only what changed. |
| The client in a browser | One request for the report, plus the spec index, outline and run index and the specs it opens. None per layer, whatever the history (measured in Chromium against a server reading S3). |

How: each layer is folded into the winning result of every check once and dropped unless it still holds a
winner, so work and memory follow the number of checks. Because the winner rule is a total order, folding in
any order is exact; a test proves the incremental report equals recomputing from every layer. The client
reads that compact report in one request and only falls back to reading every layer when you ask it to
leave a source out (which needs the history).

## 8. Troubleshooting

| You see | Cause and fix |
| --- | --- |
| `No AWS credentials found for the object store` | None of the places was set. The message lists them. `aws sso login`, or export `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`/`AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`. |
| `access denied … s3:PutObject` | The role is missing a permission. `atlas report policy --store <url>` prints the policy. |
| `403` on a layer that should not exist yet | The account cannot list the bucket (`s3:ListBucket`), so S3 answers 403 for a missing object. Grant it on the folder. |
| `the signature was rejected` | Wrong secret, or wrong region/endpoint for these keys, or the clock is off by more than 15 minutes. |
| `the bucket does not exist` | Typo, another account, or the store needs `?endpoint=…` (R2, MinIO). |
| `cannot reach <host>` | Network, DNS or endpoint. Requests are retried with backoff first. |
| The server says `listening … no backend can be read yet` | The bucket is unreachable from the server. It retries; `/readyz` stays 503 until it can read. |
| A new layer does not show | Uploaded through the server it is there at once: check the token (`401`/`403` say so). Written straight to a bucket, wait one refresh interval (10 s). Check `atlas report status --store <url>` sees it. |
| Everything is red because of one laptop | By design the newest result wins. Gate on `--ignore-modified` and a branch ([above](#5-choosing-what-takes-part)). |
| Specs are empty in the client | Nothing published with `--specs` yet, or only from a branch other than `main`: set `--outline-branch`. |
| `Run … is not shared: its privacy scan did not pass` | `--upload-run` refuses runs whose scan found real data. Fix what it found and run again. |
</doc>

<doc path="docs/report-contract.md">
# The report contract

This is the normative description of what Atlas reads and writes when it reports on specs of any
kind: Gherkin features, Quint models, DMN tables, Alloy structures, OpenSLO objectives, statecharts,
unit tests, linters, anything that ends in "this check passed or failed". If this page and the code
disagree, that is a bug: [file it](reporting-issues.md).

The contract is small on purpose. It is one document (the **layer**), one rule (how layers compose),
and one interface (the **backend** that stores them). Everything else, the client, the gate, the CLI,
is built on those three and can be replaced.

- [Concepts](#concepts)
- [The layer document](#the-layer-document)
- [How layers compose](#how-layers-compose)
- [Guarantees](#guarantees)
- [Statuses and the gate](#statuses-and-the-gate)
- [Backends](#backends)
- [Where bytes go](#where-bytes-go)
- [Versioning and stability](#versioning-and-stability)
- [Failure behaviour](#failure-behaviour)
- [Speed](#speed)
- [Other documents of the contract](#other-documents-of-the-contract)

## Concepts

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Check** | One thing a producer verified, with a stable `id` and a status: `passed`, `failed`, `running` or `not-run`. |
| **Layer** | One focused recording: the checks one **producer** ran, on one **environment**, from one version and branch, at one time. Immutable, addressed by its content. |
| **Producer** | A stable name for the suite or tool that makes layers: `gherkin`, `web-e2e`, `quint`, `openslo`. |
| **Environment** | The client that was checked: `desktop-web`, `mobile-web`, `ios`, `android`, or any other lowercase name. |
| **Slot** | The cell a check fills: producer, kind, spec, check id, environment and parameters. |
| **Backend** | A store that holds layers. Any [`ObjectStore`](#backends): a directory, a bucket, a device lab. |
| **Report** | The result of laying every layer of every backend over the current specs. Computed, never stored. |

Two ideas follow, and the rest of this page is their consequences.

1. **A report is a function of the set of layers.** There is no "the run". Nothing partitions a
   report by run, commit, branch, machine or backend; those are provenance written on each layer.
2. **Partial runs are the normal way to build a report.** A node that runs one shard, a branch that
   re-runs one scenario, a device lab that checks one environment: each publishes the layer of what it
   ran. The report fills in as layers arrive, and no node needs to know about any other.

## The layer document

`layers/manifests/<id>.json`, schema version **1**. The JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) is shipped as
[`@crvouga/atlas/schemas/layer.schema.json`](../packages/schema/schemas/layer.schema.json), and the
Zod schema as `LayerDocumentSchema` from `@crvouga/atlas/schema`.

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "id": "9f2c…64 hex digits",
  "producer": "gherkin",
  "recordedAtMs": 1760000000000,
  "sha": "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567",
  "branch": "main",
  "runUrl": "https://ci.example.com/runs/42",
  "environment": "ios",
  "parameters": { "device": "iphone-15" },
  "specs": [{ "path": "specs/join.feature", "domain": "list", "kind": "gherkin", "title": "Join a list", "fingerprint": "13:1a2b3c:4d5e6f" }],
  "parts": [{
    "id": "gherkin", "kind": "behavior", "title": "Gherkin", "recordedAtMs": 1760000000000, "sha": "0123…",
    "checks": [
      { "id": "specs/join.feature > Joins", "title": "Joins", "status": "passed", "detail": "", "specPath": "specs/join.feature", "measurements": [], "durationMs": 120 },
      { "id": "specs/join.feature > Leaves", "title": "Leaves", "status": "failed", "detail": "expected 2 members, saw 3", "specPath": "specs/join.feature", "measurements": [{ "name": "latency", "value": 1400, "unit": "ms", "limit": 2500 }] }
    ]
  }],
  "source": null,
  "recording": null,
  "bundle": {}
}
```

| Field | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `schemaVersion` | `1`. A layer without it, written before it existed, is version 1. |
| `id` | 64 lowercase hex digits: the SHA-256 of this document without `id`. Opaque to readers. The same checks recorded the same way give the same id, so publishing twice is harmless. |
| `producer` | Required, non-empty. Part of the [slot](#how-layers-compose). |
| `recordedAtMs` | When the checks ran, epoch milliseconds, `>= 0`. The newest completed result wins its slot. Take it from the test run, never from the moment of publishing, or a retried publish would claim to be newer than a later run. |
| `sha`, `branch`, `runUrl` | Provenance, or `null`. **Never part of the slot.** |
| `environment` | The client checked, or absent. Normalised to a lowercase slug: `iOS` → `ios`, `Desktop Web` → `desktop-web`, `iphone` → `ios`, `mobile browser` → `mobile-web`. Any other name is kept. Part of the slot. |
| `parameters` | Other string choices that make a result its own slot, such as `{ "device": "iphone-15" }`. A parameter named `environment` is read as the environment. Part of the slot. |
| `freshness` | `modified`: recorded from a checkout with uncommitted changes. `unknown`: origin not captured. Advisory only; see [Statuses](#statuses-and-the-gate). |
| `run` | Optional `{ id, title?, startedAtMs?, endedAtMs? }`: the execution a local or manual producer names. Layers with the same `id` in one project are one run in the run list, however many shards or batches uploaded them; a later invocation at the same branch and commit gets another `id`. Without it a run is its `runUrl`, else `branch@sha`, as before. `title` is for people. Grouping and display only: it is **never part of the slot**, never decides a winner or a status, and never hides `sha`, `branch` or `freshness`. A `run` a reader cannot read is treated as absent. |
| `specs` | The specs the layer was recorded against, with a `fingerprint` of their text, so a reader can warn when a spec changed since. Optional. |
| `parts[].kind` | An open category (`behavior`, `performance`, `accessibility`, …). A new kind needs no change to any reader. Part of the slot. |
| `parts[].checks[]` | `id` (required, stable), `title`, `status`, `detail`, `specPath`, `measurements`, `durationMs`. |
| `tags`, `labels`, `links`, `attachments`, `annotations`, `extensions` | Evidence, on the layer, a part or a check: what a result carries beyond its outcome. All optional and open. See [evidence](#evidence) and [the guide](extending.md). |
| `checks[].steps`, `checks[].attempts` | A check's timeline, and every try when it was retried. Optional. |
| `checks[].specPath` | The spec the check belongs to, as `specs/<path inside the specs directory>`. Anything before the first `specs/` is dropped, so `packages/app/specs/join.feature` and `specs/join.feature` are the same spec. |
| `measurements[]` | `{ name, value, unit, limit? }`, finite numbers. A measurement over its `limit` is shown, and never fails the check by itself. |
| `source`, `recording`, `bundle` | Optional timelines and captured files (screenshots, frames) a suite recorded. `null` and `{}` for a layer of plain checks. |

**Unknown fields are allowed and preserved.** Every object in the schema is loose. A later minor
version may add fields; an older reader ignores them and a copy carries them along.

### Evidence

A check, a part and a layer may carry evidence beyond their outcome. It is the part of the format meant to grow:
every field is optional, every object is open, every vocabulary is an open string, and none of it ever decides
a result. [Evidence: attachments, timelines, snapshots and everything else](extending.md) is the guide; the rules
are these.

| Field | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `attachments[]` | `{ name, role?, contentType?, bundleKey? \| uri? \| text?, bytes?, sha256?, width?, height?, durationMs?, description?, at?, poster?, captions?, id?, extensions? }`. A screenshot, a video, a trace, a log, a DOM snapshot, a HAR, anything. `bundleKey` is a key in the layer's `bundle` (`attachments/<sha256>`); `uri` is elsewhere; `text` is a short inline value. |
| `steps[]` | `{ id?, parentId?, name, kind?, status?, offsetMs?, durationMs?, detail?, attachments?, annotations?, extensions? }`. A flat, ordered timeline, nested by `parentId`. |
| `annotations[]` | `{ type, message, level?, at?, source?, links?, extensions? }`. |
| `attempts[]` | `{ index, status, durationMs?, startedAtMs?, detail?, steps?, attachments?, annotations?, extensions? }`. |
| `tags[]`, `labels{}`, `links[]` | Facts to filter by. `labels` are facts about the result; unlike `parameters` they never make it a different slot. |
| `extensions{}` | Structured data under a name the producer owns (`com.example.coverage`). |

The rules, which hold for every version of the format:

1. A new field is **optional**. No field is ever made required, renamed, removed or given a new meaning.
2. **Every object is open.** Unknown fields are kept at every level, and a copy carries them.
3. **Vocabularies are open.** `role`, `kind`, `type`, `level` and a step's `status` are strings with conventional
   values; an unknown one is shown generically, never rejected.
4. **Only `status`, `freshness` and `schemaVersion` are closed.** They are the whole of what decides a result.
5. **Evidence never decides a result.** A reader that cannot read a piece of evidence drops that piece and keeps
   the check, its status and its place in the report.
6. A file is stored once, in the layer, by content: `attachments/<sha256>` in `layers/blobs/`. Identical files
   attached anywhere in a layer share it, and the layer's id still depends only on what was recorded.
7. A path inside a report is data from a test run. A publisher reads the files it names only from the report's own
   folder and from folders the person chose, never a hidden file or a link out.
8. Attachment bytes are untrusted. They are served with the type the producer gave (when it is a well-formed media
   type), never sniffed, under a sandboxing content-security policy, with `cross-origin-resource-policy:
   same-origin`, and a `uri` is followed only if it is `http` or `https`.

### Choosing a check id

The check `id` is the one thing only the producer can get right, and everything depends on it: the
newer result replaces the older one only if both used the same id.

- Make it **stable** across runs: derive it from the check's identity (file, suite, name), never from
  an index, a timestamp, a random seed or a path's position in a plan.
- Make it **unique** within the layer. Publishing refuses a layer with a repeated id. When importing
  CTRF or JUnit, a repeated id gets `#2`, `#3`, … so no check is silently counted as another.
- Keep it **human**. It is what the gate prints.
- Changing an id retires the old check: its last result stays in the report until the layers that
  hold it are left out. Rename deliberately.

Atlas's own importers build ids this way:

| Source | Check id | `specPath` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CTRF | `filePath > suite… > name` (parts that exist) | `filePath`, when present |
| JUnit XML | `file or classname > name` | the `file` attribute, when present |
| Atlas run (`manifest.json`) | the path's `key`, which the same start and events give in every run | the root chart's file |
| `publishChecks` / `--checks` | whatever you give | whatever you give |

## How layers compose

A **slot** is the tuple

```
(producer, kind, specPath, check id, environment, parameters)
```

with `parameters` compared as sorted key/value pairs. Branch, commit, backend, layer id and run are
**not** in the slot. Each slot shows exactly one result: the winner among every layer that filled it.

The winner is decided by these rules, in order:

1. A **completed** result (`passed` or `failed`) beats an **unfinished** one (`running` or `not-run`),
   whatever their times. An unfinished layer never erases a completed outcome.
2. Between results of the same completeness, the **newer** `recordedAtMs` wins.
3. At the same time, **`failed` beats `passed`**, and `running` beats `not-run`. A tie fails.
4. At the same status, the greater `layerId|backendId` wins, so no input order can change the answer.

Consequences you can rely on:

- Desktop web, mobile web, iOS and Android results of the same check sit side by side.
- A layer that ran one scenario leaves every other scenario as the newest layer that ran it.
- Re-running a failing check on any branch and passing replaces the failure. Re-running and failing
  replaces the pass.
- A spec in the current specs with no layer at all stays visible as having no results. A spec that
  was removed keeps its evidence, outside the outline.
- An immutable layer held by several backends is **one** layer, reported by the backend whose id sorts
  first.
- The mutable address of an execution already held as an immutable layer is suppressed by the
  de-duplication helpers and static export. Execution identity compares producer, commit, time and
  parts; object key order at any depth does not matter, while array order does.

Leaving a layer, backend, environment, branch or version out of the input is how earlier outcomes are
inspected.

### What takes part

By default **every layer takes part**, wherever it was recorded: that is what a unified report is. The
publisher records where it came from, and the reader chooses what to include:

- `freshness` is set by the publisher from git: `modified` when the worktree has uncommitted edits to
  tracked files, `unknown` outside git, and absent for a CI checkout or a clean worktree at its commit.
  Untracked files do not count. A modified layer takes part with a warning and is never mistaken for the
  commit's own result.
- `atlas report status` and `atlas serve` (and `GET /api/status?branch=&ignoreModified=1` on a server) take `--branch <name>` (repeatable) and `--ignore-modified`
  (`ATLAS_ONLY_BRANCH`, `ATLAS_IGNORE_MODIFIED`). They only choose which layers are read; the rules above are
  unchanged. A pull request's gate is `--branch "$PR_BRANCH" --branch main --ignore-modified`: the branch
  laid over `main`, so what it did not re-run is inherited.

## Guarantees

These are tested (`packages/reports/tests/composition-laws.test.ts`, over random partial runs) and
are part of the contract:

| Guarantee | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Order independence** | The report does not depend on the order backends or layers are read in. |
| **Partition independence** | Splitting the same layers across any number of backends, machines or branches, with any overlap, gives the same report. This is what makes partial runs on separate nodes safe. |
| **Idempotence** | A layer present twice, in one backend or several, counts once. Publishing the same checks again writes the same layer. |
| **Monotonic** | A layer changes only the slots it fills. Adding a layer never changes a result it did not record. |
| **Deletion-free** | Nothing in the contract removes or rewrites a layer. Retention is the operator's choice: Atlas deletes only under a garbage collection policy an operator saved in the UI, and then only layers that no longer decide any result ([the server](server.md#user-state-and-garbage-collection)). |
| **Unknown is not a pass** | A layer that cannot be read, a backend that is down, and a check that is `running` or `not-run` never count as passing. The gate fails closed. |
| **Aggregation by copying** | Layers are immutable and never share a key with different bytes, so combining stores is copying files (`atlas report merge`, `cp -R`, `rsync`, a CI artifact download). Copying is idempotent and commutative. |

## Statuses and the gate

| Status | Meaning | Counts as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `passed` | The check ran and its expectation held. | Pass |
| `failed` | The check ran and its expectation did not hold. | Fail |
| `running` | The check has started and not finished. | Not done: fails the gate |
| `not-run` | The check was skipped, pending, blocked, or never reached. | Nothing: never a pass, never a failure |

Tools map to these four. CTRF `skipped`, `pending` and `other`, and JUnit `<skipped>`, are `not-run`.
An Atlas path that passed on retry (`flaky`) is `passed`, with the detail "Passed on retry (flaky)".

Timings that only qualify a check (parts of kind `performance`) are not counted as checks when
