anything else is recorded. A measurement over its allowance is reported and never fails a check.

**Freshness never changes a status.** A layer whose spec fingerprint no longer matches, whose
checkout was modified, or whose related code changed still shows its recorded outcome, with a
warning ("Potentially outdated: spec changed"). Atlas favours quick, possibly stale evidence over
none, and never invents a result.

### `atlas report status`

The gate passes (exit 0) only when **all** of these hold:

- at least one check has completed (`passed` or `failed`): a report where everything was skipped has
  no evidence;
- no slot's winning result is `failed`;
- no slot's winning result is `running`;
- every backend and every layer could be read (a notice is a failure);
- every environment named by `--require-environments` has at least one check;
- with `--require-all-specs`, every spec in `--specs <dir>` has at least one result.

Exit codes: `0` the report passes, `1` it does not, `2` the command itself is wrong (a store
directory that does not exist, a missing flag). A CI job can tell a broken invocation from a red report.

`--format json` prints a [`ReportStatus`](../packages/schema/schemas/report-status.schema.json)
(`schemaVersion: 1`): `ok`, `reasons`, `checks`, `byEnvironment`, `layers`, `backends`, `notices`,
`specsWithoutEvidence`, `specs` (each spec's counts, per environment) and `failing`. The text and markdown formats are for people and are not a
contract; parse the JSON.

## Backends

A backend is any implementation of `ObjectStore` (`@crvouga/atlas/reports/object-store`), seven
async methods over keys and bytes:

| Method | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `get(key)` | The object with its `contentType` and `size`, or `null` when missing. Transport errors throw. |
| `put(key, bytes, contentType)` | Idempotent: writing a key twice overwrites without error. The content type round-trips. |
| `head(key)` | `true`/`false`. Never throws for a missing key. |
| `delete(key)`, `deleteMany(keys)` | A missing key is a no-op. |
| `getUri(key)` | A URL the host can load directly, or `null`. |
| `listKeys(prefix?)` | Keys in code-unit order, optionally filtered by prefix. |
| `withPrefix(prefix)` | A store scoped to a prefix. Keys relative to it. Prefixes compose. |

It needs nothing else: no transactions, no rename, no locks, no conditional writes. That is what
lets a plain bucket, a directory and a device lab compose.

Atlas ships two backends, both named by one URL (`openStore`, `--store`, `ATLAS_STORE`):

- `directoryStore(dir)` (`@crvouga/atlas/reports/directory-store`): atomic writes, for a CI workspace, a
  mount or a laptop.
- `s3Store({ bucket, prefix, region, endpoint })` (`@crvouga/atlas/reports/s3-store`): AWS S3 and every store
  that speaks its protocol, such as R2 and MinIO, written without an SDK. `s3://bucket/folder?region=…&endpoint=…`.
  Requests are signed with Signature Version 4, retried with backoff on throttling and server errors,
  capped in flight, and follow a bucket's region. Credentials are never in a URL: they come from the
  environment the way an AWS SDK finds them. It is tested against AWS's published signing vectors and a
  live S3 server in CI. On S3 a missing object answers 403 instead of 404 for an account that cannot list
  the bucket, so publishers need `s3:ListBucket` too (`atlas report policy` prints the permissions).

For anything else, write an adapter and prove it:

```ts
import { verifyObjectStore } from '@crvouga/atlas/reports/object-store-conformance';

const { ok, failures } = await verifyObjectStore(myS3Store); // writes under a scratch prefix, cleans up
```

Several backends are one report: pass them all to `combineBackends`, to the client
(`reportsHost`), or to the CLI (`--store` for directories, `--backends <module>` for the rest). A
backend that cannot be reached is named in the notices and leaves the others usable; asking again
retries it.

## Where bytes go

All keys are relative to the backend. Layers are written **bottom up**, so a reader never meets an
entry whose content has not arrived:

A layer's checks are the contract. Next to them the store holds the two other things a whole project
needs, written the same way (content first, catalog entry last, nothing overwritten):

- **Spec sets** (`layers/specs/…`): the specs of one commit, so a client needs no checkout. A spec set is
  `{ schemaVersion, id, branch, sha, recordedAtMs, freshness?, files: [{ path, digest, fingerprint, kind,
  title, domain, bytes }] }` ([`spec-set.schema.json`](../packages/schema/schemas/spec-set.schema.json)). Its
  id is the digest of the branch, commit and file digests, so one commit's specs are one set however many
  nodes publish them. Bodies are `layers/specs/blobs/<sha256>.txt`, shared by every set that holds them.
  The outline a report is laid over is the **newest set from `main`** (then `master`, then the newest);
  a set from a modified checkout is used only if no committed set exists.
- **Run bundles** (`layers/runs/<run>/…` and `layers/runs/index/…`): a finished statechart run with its
  screenshots and clips, for the client. Uploaded only when the run's privacy scan passed; the manifest is
  written last, then the catalog entry.

The keys of a layer, bottom up:

1. `layers/blobs/<sha256>.gz`: recorded files (screenshots, frames), content-addressed and shared
   between layers. Skipped entirely for a layer of plain checks.
2. `layers/manifests/<id>.json`: the layer document, written once.
3. `layers/index/<inverted-time>-<id>.json`: `{"id": "<id>"}`, the catalog entry, written last. The
   time is inverted so a listing is newest first.

Two producers never write different bytes to one key: every key is derived from content. A crash
between steps leaves unreferenced blobs, never a catalog entry without its layer.

Everything under `layers/` is immutable and addressed by content, so `copyStore` and `atlas report merge`
carry spec sets and runs along with layers.

Stores written before layers existed (`commits/<sha>/…`, `versions/…`, `index/…`) are read in place
and composed with layers; Atlas never rewrites them. `copyStore` and `atlas report merge` copy
`layers/` only, because commit-keyed objects are mutable.

## Versioning and stability

- `schemaVersion` is the **major** version of the layer document. This is version 1.
- Within a version, changes are **additive**: a new optional field, a new open `kind`. Readers ignore
  unknown fields, so an older Atlas reads a newer minor version.
- The closed vocabularies, `status` and `freshness`, change only with a new major version. A reader
  never has to guess what an unknown status means.
- A reader reads every version **at or below its own**. A layer of a newer major version is refused by
  name ("Written with layer schema version 2; … Upgrade @crvouga/atlas") and shows up as a notice. It
  is never half understood and never counted as a pass.
- A breaking change to the document, to the [slot](#how-layers-compose) or to the
  [winner rules](#how-layers-compose) is a major version of the contract **and** a major release of
  `@crvouga/atlas` (a `!` commit). It also ships a migration note.
- Adding evidence (a new optional field, a new open vocabulary value, a new extension namespace) is a minor
  change and needs no new `schemaVersion`. `packages/reports/tests/fixtures/layer-v1-extended.json` carries every
  kind of evidence, and `layer-extensibility.test.ts` proves unknown fields survive at every level and that a
  reader of the first version of the format still reads it.
- The contract is guarded by `packages/reports/tests/fixtures/layer-v1.json`, a layer that must keep
  parsing, and by the emitted JSON Schemas, which a test keeps equal to the Zod schemas. **Never edit
  the fixture to make a test pass.**

## Failure behaviour

| What happens | What Atlas does |
| --- | --- |
| A backend is unreachable | Named in `notices` and in the backend list as unavailable; every other backend is used. The gate fails. |
| A layer is not JSON, fails the schema, or is a newer major version | Skipped with a notice naming the layer and why. The gate fails. |
| A catalog entry names a layer that is missing | A notice; the gate fails. |
| Two layers disagree | The [winner rules](#how-layers-compose) decide, the same way everywhere. |
| A publish is interrupted | Unreferenced blobs may remain. No partial layer is ever visible. Publish again. |
| A publish is retried | The same layer; nothing changes. |
| Two nodes publish at once | They write different keys, or identical bytes to the same key. |
| A required field is missing at publish | `publishChecks` throws, naming each problem by its path. Nothing is written. |
| A check id repeats within a layer | `publishChecks` throws. Importers number repeats (`#2`). |

## Speed

- Publishing a layer of plain checks is one `head` and two small writes.
- A report is one linear pass over the checks of every layer. Reading dominates it: each layer is
  one catalog read and one manifest read, a few at a time (16 by default, 64 for a node on S3).
- A long-lived reader does not redo that pass. `ReportIndex` reads each immutable layer once, folds it into
  the winning result of every slot it fills, and drops it unless it still holds a winner, so memory follows
  the number of checks (plus a few bytes for each layer ever read), not the age of the project, and a refresh
  with nothing new is one request for the newest page of the catalog. Folding is exact in any order because the winner
  rule is a total order; a test proves the incremental report equals combining every layer from scratch.
  The node sends the client only that: one request, only winning rows, with an ETag.
- Measured on a laptop with a directory backend: 300 layers of 50 checks in about 0.2 s; 1,000 layers
  of 100 checks, each recorded against 1,000 specs (100,000 results), in about 0.9 s. Composing two
  thousand layers of 100 checks (200,000 results) already in memory takes about 0.3 s.
  `performance.test.ts` holds budgets ten times looser, to catch an accidental quadratic step on a
  slow machine.
- A directory backend lists only the directories a prefix can reach. The client polls a small index,
  reads an immutable layer once and caches it forever, and loads recordings only when opened.

## Other documents of the contract

| Document | Schema | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Layer | `layer.schema.json` | What a producer publishes. This page. |
| Publish checks | `publish-checks.schema.json` | The input of `publishChecks` and `atlas report publish --checks`: a layer without the parts the publisher fills in. |
| Report status | `report-status.schema.json` | The output of `atlas report status --format json`. |
| Spec set | `spec-set.schema.json` | The specs of one commit, as published beside the layers. |
| Run manifest | `manifest.schema.json` | What `atlas run` writes for a statechart run. Publish it as a layer with `--manifest`. |
| Runs index, sources, change notices | `runs-index`, `report-sources`, `atlas-change` | How the client finds runs. See [report backends](report-backends.md). |
| CloudEvents | `cloud-event.schema.json` | Business events a run observed. |

All of them are JSON Schema 2020-12 and ship in the package at `@crvouga/atlas/schemas/<name>.schema.json`.
</doc>

<doc path="docs/extending.md">
# Evidence: attachments, timelines, snapshots and everything else

Atlas is opinionated about **specs** and open about **evidence**.

- A *spec* says what the product should do, in a notation Atlas knows how to read and show: statecharts,
  Gherkin, Quint, DMN, Alloy, OpenSLO. That list is short on purpose, and each notation gets a real view.
- *Evidence* is what a test run left behind. It is open-ended, because every framework leaves something
  different: a screenshot, a video, a Playwright trace, a HAR, a DOM or accessibility snapshot, a console
  log, a flame graph, a coverage map, a diff, a timeline of requests. Atlas stores any of it, shows what it
  can, and keeps and offers the rest.

The format is built so that a new kind of evidence **never** needs a new version of Atlas to be recorded, and
never breaks anyone who has not upgraded. This page is the model and the rules that guarantee it.

- [What a result can carry](#what-a-result-can-carry)
- [The rules that keep it compatible, forever](#the-rules-that-keep-it-compatible-forever)
- [Attach evidence](#attach-evidence)
- [What each part looks like](#what-each-part-looks-like)
- [Adding something new](#adding-something-new)

## What a result can carry

A check is a result: an `id`, a `status`, a `title`, and a `detail`. Beyond that, a check (and a layer, and a part) may
carry any of these. Every one is optional.

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `attachments[]` | Files and values: a screenshot, a video, a trace, a log, a snapshot, a HAR, a report. Any media type. |
| `steps[]` | A timeline: what happened, in order, with timing, nested with `parentId`. |
| `annotations[]` | Notes about the result: a warning, a deprecation, an accessibility finding, a coverage figure. |
| `attempts[]` | Every try, when the check was retried. |
| `tags[]` | Free labels to filter by: `smoke`, `payments`. |
| `labels{}` | Facts about the result that are not its identity: `owner`, `severity`, `browser`, `build`. |
| `links[]` | Where to read more: the CI run, the issue, the trace client. |
| `extensions{}` | Structured data of your own or a tool's, under a name you own. |
| `measurements[]` | Numbers, with units and an allowance (already part of the contract). |

An attachment may carry its own `tags[]` (`demo`): shown as `#demo` and searchable; see
[Tagging artifacts and demos](rich-evidence.md#tagging-artifacts-and-demos).

On a **layer** the same fields describe the whole run: its CI log, a coverage report, an archive of traces, the
build number, a link to the pipeline.

```json
{
  "id": "specs/checkout.feature > Pays by card",
  "title": "Pays by card",
  "status": "failed",
  "detail": "expected a receipt",
  "tags": ["smoke"],
  "labels": { "owner": "payments-team", "browser": "chromium" },
  "steps": [
    { "id": "open", "name": "Open the cart", "kind": "action", "status": "passed", "offsetMs": 0, "durationMs": 800 },
    { "id": "req", "parentId": "open", "name": "GET /cart", "kind": "request", "status": "passed", "offsetMs": 20, "durationMs": 120 },
    { "name": "Pay", "kind": "action", "status": "failed", "offsetMs": 900, "durationMs": 3000, "detail": "timeout",
      "attachments": [{ "name": "failure.png", "role": "screenshot", "contentType": "image/png", "bundleKey": "attachments/<sha256>" }] }
  ],
  "attachments": [
    { "name": "run.webm", "role": "video", "contentType": "video/webm", "bundleKey": "attachments/<sha256>", "durationMs": 4200 },
    { "name": "trace.zip", "role": "trace", "contentType": "application/zip", "uri": "https://artifacts.example.com/trace.zip" }
  ],
  "annotations": [{ "type": "accessibility", "level": "warning", "message": "Low contrast on Pay", "source": { "file": "src/pay.tsx", "line": 12 } }],
  "attempts": [{ "index": 0, "status": "failed" }, { "index": 1, "status": "failed" }],
  "extensions": { "com.example.coverage": { "lines": 0.82 } }
}
```

The complete reference, with every field, is the JSON Schema
[`layer.schema.json`](../packages/schema/schemas/layer.schema.json) (what a stored layer is) and
[`publish-checks.schema.json`](../packages/schema/schemas/publish-checks.schema.json) (what you hand to
`publishChecks` or `atlas report publish --checks`, where an attachment may name a `path` or carry `data`).

## The rules that keep it compatible, forever

These are part of [the report contract](report-contract.md#versioning-and-stability). They are why a layer
written today is readable by every Atlas to come, and a layer written by a future Atlas is readable today.

1. **Everything new is optional.** A layer with none of the fields above is as valid as it has ever been. No
   field is ever made required, renamed, removed, or given a different meaning.
2. **Every object is open.** A reader keeps and ignores fields it does not know, at every level: layer, part,
   check, step, attachment, annotation, measurement. A field added next year survives a read by an Atlas that
   does not know it, and a copy carries it along.
3. **Vocabularies are open strings.** `role`, `kind`, `type`, `level`, a step's `status` and the `kind` of a
   part have conventional values (below), not a list. A value nobody has heard of is shown generically, and
   never rejected.
4. **Only three things are closed**, and they will stay so: a check's `status` (`passed`, `failed`, `running`,
   `not-run`), `freshness`, and `schemaVersion`. Everything that decides a result is in those. Anything richer
   goes in evidence.
5. **`extensions` is yours.** Put structured data of your own under a key you own: a reverse domain
   (`com.example.coverage`) or your tool's name (`io.playwright`). Readers preserve it, show it as raw data, and
   never fail on it. Two tools cannot collide, because each uses its own name.
6. **Evidence never decides a result.** A status, a slot and a winner never depend on an attachment, a step or an
   annotation. A reader that cannot read a piece of evidence drops *that piece* and keeps the check, its status
   and the rest of its evidence. A broken screenshot reference never turns a pass into an unknown.
7. **Bytes are by reference.** A layer holds files as `bundleKey` (stored in the layer, by content, once), `uri`
   (somewhere else), or a short inline `text`. Producers never need to know how files are stored.
8. **New kinds of evidence are data.** Recording a new role, media type, annotation type or extension namespace needs no
   change to Atlas. Showing it nicely needs one renderer, and until then it is listed with its name and a
   download.

Two checks guard this in the repository: `packages/reports/tests/fixtures/layer-v1-extended.json` (a layer carrying
every kind of evidence and values from the future) and `layer-extensibility.test.ts`, which proves unknown
fields survive at every level, malformed evidence is dropped without losing the result, and a reader of the
first version of the format still reads it all.

## Attach evidence

### From the command line

```sh
# Files a CTRF report names (attachments, a base64 screenshot, stdout and stderr, steps, retries, tags) are
# read from the report's own folder and stored in the layer.
atlas report publish --producer e2e --ctrf ctrf-report.json --environment desktop-web

# Files and facts about the whole run.
atlas report publish --producer e2e --junit out.xml \
  --attach ci.log --attach trace=playwright-traces.zip \
  --label build=4821 --label browser=chromium --link 'CI=https://ci.example.com/runs/42'
```

- `--attach <file>` attaches a file to the whole layer. `--attach <role>=<file>` also gives it a role.
- `--label key=value` and `--link [name=]<url>` add facts and links about the run.
- A file the report names that cannot be found, is not allowed, or is over `--max-attachment-mb` (512) is skipped
  with a warning; the results are still published. All the files of one publish together are limited by
  `--max-total-attachment-mb` (2048), because they are held in memory while stored.
- **A report is data from a test run, not instructions.** The files it names are read only from its own folder
  and from each `--attach-root <dir>` you give; never a hidden file (`.env`, `.aws`, `.git`), never a link that
  leads out, never an absolute path elsewhere. Otherwise a test could print
  `[[ATTACHMENT|/home/runner/.aws/credentials]]` and have it uploaded. What you type with `--attach` is yours to
  choose, and is read as written.
- CTRF is mapped completely: `steps`, `attachments`, `screenshot`, `stdout`, `stderr`, `retryAttempts`, `tags`,
  `browser`, `device`, `flaky`, `snippet` and `extra`. JUnit gives each test its `<system-out>`, `<system-err>`,
  `<properties>` and Jenkins `[[ATTACHMENT|path]]` lines. An Atlas run gives each path its steps.

### From a checks file

For anything else, write what you have. `path` is read relative to the file; the same screenshot used twice is
stored once.

```json
{
  "producer": "playwright",
  "environment": "desktop-web",
  "recordedAtMs": 1760000000000,
  "labels": { "build": "4821" },
  "checks": [
    {
      "id": "specs/checkout.feature > Pays by card",
      "title": "Pays by card",
      "status": "failed",
      "detail": "expected a receipt",
      "specPath": "specs/checkout.feature",
      "tags": ["smoke"],
      "steps": [
        { "id": "open", "name": "Open the cart", "kind": "action", "status": "passed", "offsetMs": 0, "durationMs": 800 },
        { "name": "Pay", "kind": "action", "status": "failed", "offsetMs": 900, "durationMs": 3000, "attachments": [{ "name": "failure.png", "role": "screenshot", "path": "evidence/failure.png" }] }
      ],
      "attachments": [
        { "name": "run.webm", "role": "video", "path": "evidence/run.webm" },
        { "name": "console.log", "role": "log", "text": "warn: slow response" }
      ],
      "annotations": [{ "type": "accessibility", "level": "warning", "message": "Low contrast on Pay" }],
      "extensions": { "io.playwright": { "retries": 1 } }
    }
  ]
}
```

### From code

```ts
import { publishChecks } from '@crvouga/atlas/reports/publish-checks';

await publishChecks(store, {
  producer: 'e2e',
  recordedAtMs: Date.now(),
  checks: [{
    id: 'pay', title: 'Pays by card', status: 'failed',
    attachments: [
      { name: 'failure.png', role: 'screenshot', data: await Bun.file('failure.png').bytes() }, // bytes: stored in the layer
      { name: 'trace.zip', role: 'trace', uri: 'https://artifacts.example.com/trace.zip' }       // elsewhere: a reference
    ],
    steps: [{ name: 'Pay', kind: 'action', status: 'failed', offsetMs: 900, durationMs: 3000 }],
    extensions: { 'com.example.cost': { cents: 3 } }
  }]
});
```

Give bytes as `data` (or `base64`, or a long `text`); the publisher stores them in the layer by content,
fills in `bundleKey`, `bytes` and `sha256`, and removes what you handed over. Identical files are stored once.
Publishing the same input twice writes the same layer.

## What each part looks like

**Attachments** are shown by what they are, from their media type:

| Media type | Shown as |
| --- | --- |
| `image/*` | A picture, opening full size |
| `video/*` | A video with controls, seekable (range requests) |
| `audio/*` | An audio player |
| `text/html` | A page snapshot in a frame with no permissions: nothing in it can run |
| `application/pdf` | A frame |
| `text/*`, JSON, XML, YAML | The text, pretty-printed for JSON, up to 200 000 characters |
| anything else | Its name, its role, its type and size, and a download |

Attachment bytes are served as untrusted: never sniffed, with a sandboxing policy, never embeddable by another site.
An attachment's `uri` is followed only if it is an `http` or `https` address.

**Steps** are a flat list: order them by `offsetMs`, nest them by `parentId`. Whatever your framework calls them
(actions, hooks, requests, spans, Given/When/Then) they fit. **Annotations** show their `level` (`info`,
`warning`, `error`; any other level is shown as written) and where in the source they point.
**Extensions** you add appear as raw data under the result, so nothing a tool recorded is out of reach.

Conventional values, in case you want to be understood by others: attachment `role`: `screenshot`, `video`,
`trace`, `log`, `snapshot`, `har`, `coverage`, `diff`, `report`, `captions`. Step `kind`: `action`,
`assertion`, `hook`, `request`, `span`, `given`, `when`, `then`. Step `status`: `passed`, `failed`, `skipped`.
Annotation `type`: `note`, `warning`, `deprecation`, `issue`, `accessibility`, `coverage`.

## Adding something new

| You want to record | Do |
| --- | --- |
| A kind of file Atlas has never seen | Attach it with its media type and a `role`. It is stored and offered for download today. |
| Structured data of your own | Put it in `extensions` under a name you own. It is kept, and shown as raw data. |
| A new annotation type, role or step kind | Use it. Open vocabularies need no registration. |
| Something that should be shown well | Ask for a renderer (below). |
| A field every tool should have | Open an issue. It is added as an optional field, and the rules above guarantee nothing breaks. |

**A renderer** is one entry in the client's list (`artifactRenderers` in
`packages/visualizer/src/evidence/artifacts.tsx`): how to show an attachment of a media type. The first one that
matches wins:

```tsx
registerArtifactRenderer({
  id: 'flamegraph',
  matches: (attachment, mediaType) => mediaType === 'application/x-flamegraph',
  render: (attachment, { url }) => <FlameGraph src={url} />
});
```

The client is part of Atlas, so a renderer for a new media type is a contribution to Atlas: file an issue
([reporting issues](reporting-issues.md)) with a sample file. Until it lands, the attachment is still stored,
listed with its name, role, type and size, and offered for download, and everything else about the result is
unaffected.
</doc>

<doc path="docs/report-backends.md">

</doc>

<doc path="docs/statecharts.md">
# Executable statecharts

Write down how a product behaves as statecharts in open formats, then let Atlas lint them, plan
paths that cover every transition, run those paths against the real product through any driver (a
browser, a phone, a plain function), and write a manifest of what happened, with screenshots, video
clips, captions, business events and standard test reports. Each run publishes as a layer
(`atlas report publish --manifest`), so it combines with every other suite's evidence. This page covers
running them, from a runnable example to the Atlas client.

```
specs/                     atlas lint      the charts are pure, reachable, free of silent dead ends,
  app.scxml          ──▶                   and every journey replays
  child.machine.yaml       atlas plan      curated journeys + shortest paths covering every transition
  journeys.yaml            atlas run       each path against the product, through a driver
                                  │
                                  ▼
                           atlas-runs/<run>/manifest.json, junit.xml, ctrf.json, chart.mmd, media/
```

The spec is the source of truth for the product's behaviour, not for the test code: a state says
what a person sees, an event says what happens in business language ("Adds a todo", "Sync fails"),
and the implementation says how a driver makes each event happen and recognises each state.

## Quick start: the todo example

[`examples/todo`](https://github.com/crvouga/atlas/tree/main/examples/todo) is a dependency-free web app (static HTML and vanilla JavaScript
served by a small Node server) specified as two charts:

- `specs/todo-app.scxml`, the root chart in SCXML: a welcome screen, a "Setting up" state that
  invokes the child chart, and a `<parallel>` "Working on the list" state whose "Sync" and "List"
  regions change independently.
- `specs/getting-started.machine.yaml`, the child chart in XState YAML. Its two final states hand
  back to the parent through `meta.doneEvent`.
- `specs/journeys.yaml`, four curated journeys.
- `specs/getting-started.feature` and `specs/working-the-list.feature`, the same stories in Gherkin.
- `specs/todo.qnt`, the list, its sync, and its actions as a Quint model.

The Atlas client lists the features under Gherkin and the model under Quint.

It has every kind of event: user events (taps and typing), a **system** event ("Sync fails", which
the test triggers through a real HTTP endpoint on the example server), a **time** event ("Retry
timer elapses", which jumps Playwright's clock 30 seconds) and **hand-off** events from the child
chart. The server reports business events as CloudEvents to an Atlas `cloudEventsHttpSource`, so
the states' `meta.events` are checked on every run.

This repository runs on [Bun](https://bun.sh). Video clips and WebP thumbnails need FFmpeg on the
`PATH`. From the repository root:

```sh
bun install
bunx playwright install chromium

bun run example:lint   # pure, reachable, no undocumented dead ends, journeys replay, everything implemented
bun run example:plan   # 4 journeys + 1 generated path cover all 14 transitions
bun run example:fast   # run every path quickly
bun run example:run    # statechart showcase, then the Gherkin features and the Quint model
bun test examples      # the same spec against an in-memory model, as a test suite

bun run example:clients      # clients/: one chart across a phone, a desktop and the sync server at once
bun run example:clients:bun  # the same, with the desktop in Bun's WebKit and the phone in Playwright's Chromium
```

To run every chart of the example and browse the results, run these in separate terminals; the
visualizer updates when a run finishes.

```sh
bun run atlas:run   # example:clients, then example:run: every chart of the example, in showcase mode
bun atlas          # the example's specs, chart runs, and layered reports
```

Each config writes its own run and the Atlas client shows one run at a time: the latest is the
single-browser run, and the run across clients is the one before it in the run picker.

Gherkin, Quint, DMN, Alloy and OpenSLO documents sit beside the charts. Results compose across
environments, branches and backends within each project. **Sources** switches report sources on or off.

`bun atlas` runs the singleton Atlas server and the client together at `http://localhost:5180`.
It starts a project-agnostic node with no example data. Select a project using the top-right picker.
In another terminal run `bun run example:run`: statecharts, Gherkin scenarios and Quint traces stream running checks, completed results and current steps
to project `todo-app` on that server while testing. Producers renew a heartbeat every 5 seconds; 30 seconds of silence
marks an invocation interrupted. Final specs and recordings upload when their privacy scan completes.
Tests show inline running indicators and logs without waiting for the whole suite to finish. Report history
is retained in the server's bucket under `projects/todo-app/`; local run artifacts remain in `atlas-runs` and
`atlas-reports`. To upload a completed run again without rerunning tests,
use `bun run example:publish`. Set `ATLAS_SERVER_URL` for a different upload destination (and
`ATLAS_PUBLISH_TOKEN` when it requires one). Restart `bun atlas` when switching from the older
file-based example client; a busy port is an error so publishers cannot silently target another server.

A showcase run ends with:

```
States 14/14 passed, 0 failed, 0 not reached
Transitions 14/14 passed, 0 failed, 0 not reached
Manifest: examples/todo/atlas-runs/<run-id>/manifest.json
```

`example:run` then runs the Gherkin features in a browser and the Quint model, and streams every scenario and trace as it runs, including sharing and renaming. The final recordings are uploaded alongside the completed statechart run.

`bun test examples` runs [`model.test.ts`](https://github.com/crvouga/atlas/blob/main/examples/todo/model.test.ts): the same charts and journeys
against `TodoModel`, a plain class, through `functionDriver` and `describeAtlas`. Only the driver
and the implementation differ, which is the point: the spec belongs to the product, not to one
test tool.

## Writing specs

### Files

Atlas loads every chart and journeys file directly inside the specs directory:

- `*.scxml`, `*.machine.json`, `*.machine.yaml` (or `.yml`): one chart each;
- `journeys.yaml` (or `.yml`, `.json`): the curated journeys.

The **root** chart is the one no other chart invokes. A chart's id is the SCXML `name` attribute or
the XState `id`.

### The pure subset

Atlas walks charts without running any code, so it executes only the parts of a statechart that
are pure structure:

- states, nesting (`initial`), `parallel` regions and `final` states;
- event transitions, written as a target (`Opens: Open` or `{ target: '#Open' }`), with
  optional declarative metadata (`{ target: '#Open', meta: { source: ['specs/door.feature'] } }`);
- `invoke` that names another chart (`src`, `id`, `onDone`), composed statically;
- `meta`.

Guards, actions, `entry`/`exit`, `context`, `after` (delays), `always`, `output` and `onError` are
lint errors. A condition becomes a state or an event instead: "Payment declined" is an event the
system sends, not a guard on "Pays"; "30 seconds pass" is a time event, not an `after`.

State names are global across the composed product (transitions target `#<name>`), so they must be
unique across charts, and they cannot contain dots. Names are business language and may contain
spaces.

### `meta`

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `description` | What is true in this state. Required on every state by default (`requiredMeta` changes that). |
| `snapshot` | What a person sees, in words. |
| `events` | Business events that happen on entering the state, checked against what event sources observed. |
| `checks` | Things to verify on screen, quoted from the spec; the implementation's `checks()` returns their results. |
| `confidence` | `confirmed` or `assumed`. |
| `source` | Where the behaviour is documented. |
| `deadEnd` | Why a state with no way out is meant to be one. Without it, a dead end is a lint error. |
| `doneEvent` | On a child chart's final state: the event its parent receives from that final. |
| `childMachine`, `childFinalEvents` | Legacy composition on the parent state. Prefer `invoke`. |

### SCXML conventions

SCXML ids are XML IDs and event attributes are token lists, so business names travel in an
`atlas:name` attribute next to a token id. Metadata lives in the `atlas` namespace, as SCXML allows:

```xml
<scxml xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/07/scxml" xmlns:atlas="https://github.com/crvouga/atlas/ns/1"
       version="1.0" datamodel="null" name="Todo app" initial="welcome">
  <state id="welcome" atlas:name="Welcome">
    <atlas:meta>
      <atlas:description>The first screen a person sees.</atlas:description>
      <atlas:event>App opened</atlas:event>
    </atlas:meta>
    <transition event="starts-setup" atlas:name="Starts setup" target="setting-up"/>
  </state>
  <state id="setting-up" atlas:name="Setting up">
    <atlas:meta><atlas:description>The child chart runs here.</atlas:description></atlas:meta>
    <invoke id="getting-started" src="getting-started.machine.yaml" atlas:name="Getting started"/>
    <transition event="done.invoke.getting-started" target="working"/>
  </state>
  ...
</scxml>
```

`<atlas:event>`, `<atlas:check>` and `<atlas:source>` repeat to form lists; `<atlas:dead-end>` is
`meta.deadEnd`; a final state's `atlas:done-event` attribute is `meta.doneEvent`. `atlas export
--format scxml` writes any chart (or the composed product) back out in this form, and reading it
again gives the same chart.

### Composition

A parent state runs a child chart with any of:

1. XState `invoke: { src: 'Child', id: 'child', onDone: '#Next' }`, or SCXML `<invoke id="child">`
   plus a `done.invoke.child` transition;
2. `meta.doneEvent` on the child's final states, each naming the event the parent receives, which
   the parent handles in its `on` (a final whose event the parent does not handle goes to
   `onDone`);
3. legacy `meta.childMachine: 'Child'` and `meta.childFinalEvents: { <final>: <event> }` on the
   parent state.

Atlas inlines each child into the state that invokes it. The child's final states stay as states
(so they keep their screenshots and checks) but take the parent's transition for their hand-off
event. When a path reaches one, the hand-off happens by itself: journeys never list hand-off
events, and the planner inserts them. Give each hand-off event an implementation of kind
`hand-off` (usually a no-op); events without an implementation count as blocked.

### Journeys

```yaml
journeys:
  Keeps working through a sync outage:
    description: Adds todos while the sync is down, and the retry catches up.
    events: [Starts setup, Skips naming the list, Adds a todo, Sync fails, Adds a todo, Retry timer elapses]
    endsIn: [Some todos open, Synced]
```

The linter replays each journey through the composed chart and checks it ends in every `endsIn`
state. Each journey runs as its own path; generated paths only cover what journeys leave out.

## Implementing a spec

An implementation tells a driver how to make each event happen and how to recognise each state.
Events are keyed by their exact name in the spec.

```ts
import { defineConfig } from '@crvouga/atlas';
import { playwrightDriver, role, screen, text } from '@crvouga/atlas/playwright';

export default defineConfig({
  specs: './specs',
  driver: () => playwrightDriver({ clock: true }),
  targets: ['http://127.0.0.1:4317'],
  implementation: {
    async setup({ page }) {
      await page.goto('http://127.0.0.1:4317');
    },
    events: {
      'Adds a todo': {
        kind: 'user',
        how: 'Types a todo and taps "Add".',
        async run({ page, user }) {
          await user.type(page.getByLabel('New todo'), 'Water the plants', 'New todo');
          await user.tap(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add' }), 'Add');
        }
      },
      'Retry timer elapses': {
        kind: 'time',
        how: 'Jumps the page clock 30 seconds.',
        run: ({ page }) => page.clock.fastForward(30_000)
      }
    },
    states: {
      'No todos': screen({ all: [text('Nothing to do yet')] }),
      Offline: screen({ all: [text('Offline')], none: [text('All changes synced')] })
    }
  }
});
```

**Events** (`EventImplementation<C>`): `kind` is `user`, `system`, `time` or `hand-off`; `how` is a
plain-language note shown in reports; `run(ctx, tools)` makes it happen; `prepare(ctx, tools)`
creates test data before the path starts; `blocked: '<reason>'` marks an event that cannot run yet,
so paths stop before it and report why.

**States** (`StateImplementation<C>`): `recognize(ctx)` returns whether the state is showing and the
signals it looked at. Optional: `checks(ctx)` (results for `meta.checks`; a failed check fails the
state), `lookIn(ctx)` (where to look when the change happens off screen, such as reloading or
opening another tab), `settle(ctx)` (within-state actions after the screenshot, such as
dismissing a toast), `transient` (shown too briefly to wait for) and `sameAs` (a state the UI cannot
tell apart from this one).

**Setup**: `setup(ctx, { path, tools })` puts the product in the path's start configuration;
`canStart(active)` returns `true` or the reason a start configuration cannot be set up yet. It is
optional when seeds cover every start.

**Seeds** (`seeds: Record<string, Seed<C>>`): see [Seeds and parallel runs](#seeds-and-parallel-runs).

**Correlation**: `correlate(ctx)` returns ids (a user id, a trace id) that tell this attempt's
business events from those of attempts running beside it.

Only leaf states need recognisers. `atlas lint --require-implementations` lists every event and
leaf state in scope that has no implementation.

## Seeds and parallel runs

A chart of a whole product is deep: a member reaches a results screen after signing up,
onboarding, paying and booking. Walking every path from the initial state repeats that prefix
in every path, so a run gets slower the more of the product it covers. Seeds remove the prefix.

A seed puts the system directly in one configuration of the chart, usually through an API or the
database: create a member who has paid, sign them in, open the screen.

```ts
implementation: {
  seeds: {
    'Paid member': {
      at: 'Paid',                               // a state name, or a full state value
      how: 'Creates a paid member through the admin API and signs in.',
      async run({ page, api }) {
        const member = await api.createMember({ plan: 'paid' });
        await page.goto(`/sign-in?token=${member.token}`);
      }
    }
  },
  events: { /* … */ },
  states: { /* … */ }
}
```

With seeds, the plan changes in three ways:

- **Journeys are cut at seeded configurations.** A journey is replayed from the initial state, and
  wherever it passes through a configuration a seed produces, it is cut. Each stretch becomes a path
  that starts from that seed. A stretch that several journeys share becomes one path. The manifest's
  `journeys` lists the paths each journey is made of. A journey passes when all of them pass, fails
  when one fails, and is `not-reached` while any is blocked.
- **Generated paths start from the nearest seed.** A breadth-first search from every start point at
  once finds, for each uncovered transition, the shortest way to take it from any seed (or from
  `setup`'s start). Ties go to the seed declared first.
- **Redundant paths are dropped.** A generated path that is a prefix of another path from the same
  start is not planned.

The plan is deterministic. The same chart, journeys and seeds give the same paths, ids and keys
(`key` hashes the start and the events) on every machine, so results can be composed:

- **Workers.** `--workers n` (or `workers` in the config) runs n path attempts at once. Each attempt
  gets its own driver context. The longest paths go first, timed by earlier runs.
  - The driver's `concurrency` caps the worker count. Playwright and Bun contexts and HTTP clients
    run side by side. A WebDriver session or a Detox device runs one at a time unless you raise it.
  - The manifest is a pure fold of the path outcomes in plan order, so the same outcomes give the
    same report whatever order they finished in.
- **Shards.** `--shard i/n` runs one part of the plan, split by the plan alone, so every machine
  agrees on the split. `atlas merge <run-dir>...` composes the shards into one run, with their media
  copied in.
- **Reruns.** `--rerun-failed` keeps the passed paths of the newest run, matched by key, and runs
  the rest. The result is still one complete run.
- **Areas.** `--seed <name>` (repeatable) runs only the paths that start from that seed (`start`
  for paths `setup` starts). `--state <name>` scopes the run to one state of the chart. With these you can
  run one area of the product on its own, then merge it into a full run.

Seeds are what make the composition sound: a seed must leave the system exactly as the steps that
lead there would. Atlas checks this both ways and reports it:
- A seeded path must first recognise its start state.
- The manifest's `seeds` lists, for each seed, the passed paths that reached the same states through
  real steps (`verifiedBy`).

A seed nobody reaches through the steps is a claim that has not been checked yet. In the
visualizer, seeded states carry a "Seeded" tag.

Business events and parallel runs: a shared source, such as a log file, sees every attempt's events.
`EventSource.mark()` returns a position that `collect(mark)` reads from, so attempts don't consume
each other's marks.
- With `correlate(ctx)`, only events and log lines that mention one of the attempt's ids count.
- Without it, a run on several workers reports business events as "no signal" rather than guessing.

## Drivers

| Driver | Package | Plays | Speed | Clips |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `functionDriver(create)` | `@crvouga/atlas` | A domain model, a CLI, anything reachable from code | Microseconds | No |
| `httpDriver(baseUrl)` | `@crvouga/atlas` | An API client with a cookie jar: a partner system, an operator API, a back office job | Milliseconds | No |
| `bunWebViewDriver()` | `@crvouga/atlas/bun` | A web app in Bun's built-in browser (WebKit on macOS, Chrome elsewhere) | A view in milliseconds, screenshots in about 10 ms | From screenshots |
| `playwrightDriver()` | `@crvouga/atlas/playwright` | A web app (or React Native on the web) in Chromium, with a fake clock | About a second per context | Screencast with a touch overlay |
| `webdriverDriver()` | `@crvouga/atlas/webdriver` | Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge; native iOS and Android apps through Appium | Depends on the server | From screenshots, or Appium's recorder |
| `detoxDriver()` | `@crvouga/atlas/detox` | A React Native app, inside a Detox test run | Depends on the device | Detox artifacts |

The Bun, Playwright, WebDriver and Detox contexts all provide a `SignalContext` (`goto`,
`isVisible`, `user.tap`, `user.type`), and they resolve the same signals (`testId`, `role`, `label`,
`text`, `css` from `@crvouga/atlas/signals`), each against its own UI tree: the DOM, or the
accessibility tree of a native app, where a test ID is the accessibility identifier (React
Native's `testID`). An implementation written
against `SignalContext` with `screen` from `@crvouga/atlas/signals` runs on any of them unchanged.

`bunWebViewDriver` needs the Bun runtime: run `bun --bun atlas run`. The `atlas` binary runs on
Node (through tsx) or Bun, and Playwright works under Bun too, so one run can mix Bun's WebKit and
Playwright's Chromium.

## Several clients in one run

Product flows cross devices: a member books on an iOS app, an operator approves in a web
dashboard, a partner confirms over an API. `combineDrivers` runs several drivers as the named
clients of one run, and `combineImplementations` merges what each client does and shows:

```ts
import { combineDrivers, combineImplementations, defineConfig, httpDriver, type HttpClient } from '@crvouga/atlas';
import { role, screen, text, type SignalContext } from '@crvouga/atlas/signals';
import { playwrightDriver } from '@crvouga/atlas/playwright';
import { accessibilityId, webdriverDriver } from '@crvouga/atlas/webdriver';

type Clients = { member: SignalContext; operator: SignalContext; partner: HttpClient };

export default defineConfig<Clients>({
  specs: './specs',
  driver: combineDrivers<Clients>(
    {
      member: webdriverDriver({
        url: 'http://127.0.0.1:4723', // Appium
        capabilities: { platformName: 'iOS', 'appium:automationName': 'XCUITest', 'appium:app': './build/App.app' }
      }),
      operator: playwrightDriver({ baseUrl: 'http://127.0.0.1:3000', device: { viewport: { width: 1280, height: 800 } } }),
      partner: httpDriver('http://127.0.0.1:4000')
    },
    { screens: 'all' }
  ),
  implementation: combineImplementations<Clients>(
    {
      member: {
        events: { 'Requests a visit': { kind: 'user', how: 'Taps "Request".', run: (m) => m.user.tap(role('button', 'Request'), 'Request') } },
        states: { 'Visit confirmed': screen({ all: [text('Confirmed')] }) }
      },
      operator: {
        setup: (o) => o.goto('/queue'),
        events: { 'Operator approves': { kind: 'user', how: 'Approves it in the queue.', run: (o) => o.user.tap(role('button', 'Approve'), 'Approve') } },
        states: { 'Waiting for approval': screen({ all: [role('row', 'New request')] }) }
      },
      partner: {
        events: { 'Partner confirms': { kind: 'system', how: 'POSTs the confirmation webhook.', run: (p) => p.post('/webhooks/confirm', { ok: true }).then(() => undefined) } }
      }
    },
    { setup: async ({ partner }) => void (await partner.post('/test/reset')) }
  )
});
```

- Each client's part is written against that client's own context, so every driver's helpers
  work unchanged; `shared` (the second argument) holds setup and events that need several clients
  at once. `shared.setup` runs first, then each client's setup in order.
- `onClient(name, impl)` lifts a single event or state implementation to a client.
- An event's client is recorded for its clip; a state's client is the screen it is recognised and
  photographed on. With `screens: 'all'`, every other client's screen is captured at the same
  moment (`screenshot.also`).
- Timeline entries, clips, states and transitions carry `client` in the manifest;
  `run.environment.clients` names the driver each client ran on; a failed attempt keeps one trace
  per client.
- If one client cannot open (no simulator booted), the others are closed and the attempt fails
  naming that client.

[`examples/todo/clients`](https://github.com/crvouga/atlas/tree/main/examples/todo/clients) runs a chart (`specs/clients/shared-list.scxml`)
across a phone, a desktop and the sync server; pick each device's driver with `ATLAS_PHONE` and
`ATLAS_DESKTOP` (`playwright`, `bun` or `webdriver`).

## Writing a driver

A driver owns the thing under test for one path attempt: a browser context, a device, a model or
an API client. Only `open` and `close` are required.

```ts
type Focus = { client?: string };

type Driver<C> = {
  name: string;
  open(input: { path: PlannedPath; attempt: number; mode: RunMode; directory: string; timeline: Timeline }): Promise<C>;
  close(ctx: C, input: { failed: boolean; traceFile: string }): Promise<{ trace?: string; traces?: Record<string, string> } | void>;
  screenshot?(ctx: C, file: string, focus?: Focus): Promise<Image | null>;
  record?(ctx: C, workDirectory: string, focus?: Focus): Promise<{ stop(output: string): Promise<Clip | null> }>;
  text?(ctx: C, focus?: Focus): Promise<string>;
  hold?(ctx: C, ms: number, focus?: Focus): Promise<void>;
  pacing?: { before: number; after: number };
  clients?: Record<string, string>;
  concurrency?: number;
  dispose?(): Promise<void>;
};
```

`focus` says which client a multi-client run is looking at; single-client drivers ignore it.
A driver without a native screen recorder can encode clips from screenshots with
`recordFrames(capture, workDirectory)`.

- `open` returns a fresh context for each attempt; `close` may return the path of a trace file
  (Playwright writes one for failed attempts).
- `screenshot` and `record` produce media; `record` is used only in showcase mode, one clip per
  transition.
- `text` returns the visible text, for the privacy scan.
- `concurrency` is how many contexts can be open at once (1 when omitted). Workers never exceed
  it, so a driver of one device stays sequential while browser contexts run side by side.
- `timeline.add({ kind, label, ... })` logs taps, typing, system calls and time jumps; they become
  each clip's captions.

For anything you can reach from Node (a domain model, an API client, a CLI), `functionDriver(create)`
is a complete driver:

```ts
import { functionDriver } from '@crvouga/atlas';

const driver = functionDriver(() => new TodoModel());
```

## CLI

```
atlas lint   [--config atlas.config.ts | --specs <dir>] [--require-implementations]
atlas plan   [--config atlas.config.ts] [--state <name>]
atlas run    [--config atlas.config.ts] [--mode fast|showcase] [--workers n] [--state <name>]
             [--seed <name>]... [--paths id,id] [--shard i/n] [--rerun-failed | --reuse <run-dir>]
             [--no-retry] [--output <dir>]
atlas merge  [--config atlas.config.ts] [--output <dir>] <run-dir> <run-dir>...
atlas export --specs <dir> --format scxml|mermaid|markdown|json [--out <file>]
atlas report publish|stream|status|merge|doctor|policy …   layered evidence for any kind of spec (below)
```

- `lint` with `--specs` checks charts and journeys alone; with a config it also lists missing
  implementations, and `--require-implementations` makes them errors.
- `plan` prints the seeds and each path with:
  - its seed and step count;
  - what blocks it;
  - the paths each journey is made of;
  - the total and longest path length, and how many transitions stay uncovered.
- `run` exits non-zero when a path fails or the privacy scan finds something. `--paths` runs only
  the given path ids; `--no-retry` skips the retry of failed paths.
- `--workers`, `--shard`, `--seed`, `--state`, `--rerun-failed` and `--reuse` are described in
  [Seeds and parallel runs](#seeds-and-parallel-runs).
- `merge` composes runs of the same plan (shards, or a rerun and its earlier run) into one run.
- `export` writes the composed product (every child inlined) as SCXML, Mermaid, Markdown or
  XState JSON. The Markdown is a readable map for the people who own the product: one section per
  area (each parallel region apart), every state with its description and what the user sees (a
  `snapshot` written as an identifier is left out), a table of every event that can happen there
  and where it leads, then the named journeys.

The config file is TypeScript (loaded with `tsx`) and defaults to `atlas.config.ts` in the current
directory. Relative paths in it resolve against the config file's directory.

### `atlas report`

Evidence for specs of any kind, not only statecharts: `publish`, `status`, `merge`, `doctor`, `policy`
and `stream`. Run `atlas report --help` for every flag. [Integrating Atlas](integrating.md) is the guide,
[running Atlas for a project](deploying.md) covers the server, S3 and filters, and
[the report contract](report-contract.md) holds the rules. For a statechart run:

```sh
atlas report publish --producer statecharts --environment desktop-web \
  --manifest atlas-runs/<run>/manifest.json --specs ./specs --upload-run
```

`--upload-run` also sends the run's screenshots and clips to the store (or the server) so the client can show them
(only when the run's privacy scan passed).

## Config reference

`defineConfig<C>(config)` returns the config unchanged, typed for the driver's context `C`.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `specs` | The specs directory. |
| `driver` | A `Driver<C>`, or a function returning one (called once per run). |
| `implementation` | `{ events, states, seeds?, setup?, canStart?, correlate? }`. |
| `chart` | Run one chart of the product; the root chart when omitted. |
| `start`, `startLabel` | Where generated paths start (an XState state value) and how to describe it; the initial state when omitted. |
| `entryEvents` | When running one chart or one state: the only events that enter it from outside. |
| `state` | Run one state of a chart and what is inside it, with the transitions into and out of it: one area of a chart that models the whole product. |
| `workers` | Path attempts that run at once, capped by the driver's `concurrency`; one per CPU when omitted. |
| `beforeRun` | Runs once before any path: prepare what every seed relies on (reference data, configuration). |
| `output` | Where runs are written; `atlas-runs` beside the config. |
| `eventSources` | `() => EventSource[]`: where business events come from. |
| `eventMatchers` | How each business event name is recognised: `{ type }`, `{ pattern }` or a function. |
| `privacy` | Extra `deny` patterns, `allowEmails` and `allowHosts`. |
| `targets` | URLs the run reaches, checked against `privacy.allowHosts` before anything runs. |
| `environment` | Recorded in the manifest. |
| `stepTimeoutMs` | How long to wait for a state to show up (default 45 000). |
| `requiredMeta` | `meta` fields every state needs (default `['description']`). |

The programmatic API mirrors the CLI: `prepare(config)` loads, lints and plans; `runConfig(config,
options)` runs; `loadSpecDirectory`, `lintBundle`, `chartScope`, `planChart` and `runPaths` are the
steps underneath.

## How a run works

1. **Plan.** Curated journeys come first.
   - When running one chart of a larger product, each journey is cut to its stretch inside the
     chart, starting at an entry transition.
   - With seeds, journeys are also cut wherever they pass through a seeded configuration.
   - Then, for each transition still uncovered, the plan adds the shortest path that takes it from
     the nearest seed or start. The search is breadth-first, so loops stay bounded.
   - Paths stop before blocked events. A blocked path whose runnable part other paths already cover
     is reported but not run.
2. **Run each path.** Paths run on a pool of workers, longest first. Each gets a fresh driver
   context, then every event's `prepare`, then its seed's `run` (or `setup`). The start state must
   be recognised. Then for each step: run the event, wait for the target state, run its checks,
   collect business events, screenshot, `settle`.
3. **Retry.** A failed path runs once more. Passing the second time makes it `flaky`.
4. **Write.** The manifest and reports are rewritten each time a path finishes, from every outcome
   so far in plan order, so a crash keeps what ran. `outcomes.json` keeps the raw outcomes, for
   `atlas merge` and `--rerun-failed`.

Every path, state and transition ends as `passed`, `failed`, `flaky` or `not-reached`. Reaching a
state also reaches its ancestors. A failure records the recogniser's signals and which known states
the screen looked like instead.

### Run modes

| Mode | Pacing | Media |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fast` | None | Screenshots of every state (when the driver takes them) |
| `showcase` | Holds before and after each step; taps glide and type at human speed | Screenshots, plus an H.264 clip of every transition with a poster and WebVTT captions |

## Manifest and reports

Each run writes `<output>/<timestamp>-<mode>/`:

| File | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `manifest.json` | The run (commit, branch, environment, mode, spec version, scope), every chart, the composed map (nodes and edges), every state and transition with status, media, timeline and reasons, every path with its attempts, coverage and privacy results. Schema: `packages/schema/schemas/manifest.schema.json`. |
| `junit.xml` | One test case per path: failures, skips (with the blocking reason) and flaky passes. |
| `ctrf.json` | The same as CTRF. |
| `chart.mmd` | The composed chart as a Mermaid state diagram. |
| `outcomes.json` | Each path's raw outcome by path key, which the manifest is folded from: for merging shards and reusing passed paths. |
| `media/paths/<path>/NN.png`, `.webp` | Screenshots of each state a path reached; `failed-NN.png` where it failed. |
| `media/clips/<path>/NN.mp4`, `.poster.webp`, `.vtt` | Showcase clips of each transition, with captions. |
| `media/traces/<path>.zip` | Driver traces of failed attempts (Playwright traces with the Playwright driver). |

A run is also evidence for the report. `atlas report publish --manifest <run>/manifest.json` turns it
into a layer with one check per path, identified by the path's `key` (the same start and events give
the same key in every run). `atlas merge` composes the shards of one plan into one *run*; layers
compose a run with everything else: other suites, other environments, other branches.

## Business events

States list the business events that happen on entering them in `meta.events`. An `EventSource`
says what actually happened. `mark()` returns a position before each event, and `collect(mark)`
returns what arrived after it, once the state is recognised:

- `cloudEventsHttpSource()` starts an HTTP endpoint that accepts CloudEvents in structured, binary
  or batch mode. Point the product's event bus, webhook relay or collector at its `url`.
- `logFileSource(file)` collects lines appended to a log, for products whose only event stream is a
  log; match them with `{ pattern }`.
- Any object with `name`, `mark` and `collect` works, such as an in-memory bus in a unit test.

With no matcher, a business event is observed when a CloudEvent's `type` equals its name. Events
with neither a matcher nor a CloudEvents source are reported as "no signal", never as missing.

## Privacy

Runs produce media and manifests that get shared, so Atlas refuses to leak real data:

- Before running, every `targets` URL must be on `allowHosts` (loopback only by default).
- After every step, the driver's visible text is scanned, and the manifest is scanned before it is
  written. By default it flags email addresses outside `example.com`/`.org`/`.net` and the `.test`,
  `.example`, `.invalid`, `.localhost` and `.local` domains, anything shaped like a US Social Security
  number, and card numbers other than the well-known test cards. Findings describe the match without
  repeating it.
- Any finding fails the run. Add `deny` patterns and `allowEmails` in `privacy`.

## Visualizer

The [`atlas client`](../packages/visualizer) command renders the charts from the specs directory and
overlays runs from the runs directory: screenshots on states, clips on transitions, statuses and
history. See its README for how to point it at a project.

Its open index lists every place, journey and spec beside one plate. Connect multiple local
directories, HTTP report stores and streaming
APIs using [report backends](report-backends.md). The runner publishes reached screens
and completed steps while paths are still running.

Layered reports for any spec appear beside the charts: each Gherkin, Quint, DMN, Alloy and OpenSLO
document shows the combined result of its checks per environment, with the layer behind each. Point
the client at your stores with `reportsHost` ([integrating Atlas](integrating.md#6-browse-it)).
</doc>

<doc path="docs/workspaces.md">
# Atlas in agent IDEs

This guide is for developing **this repository** in Superset, super.engineering or Orca. A consumer
project should install Atlas from npm and follow [integrating](integrating.md) instead.

## Start from any terminal

Install the Bun version named by `packageManager` in [package.json](../package.json), then run these
commands from the repository root. Setup requires no tokens, copied `.env`, Docker or external services.

```sh
bun run workspace:setup
bun run workspace:run
```

Open the `Atlas server ready:` URL printed in the Run terminal. It serves the real API and hot-reloading
viewer together; `/admin` opens settings. A fresh node starts empty. Publish real results to the printed
`ATLAS_STORE` address using the existing [report commands](reference/reports.md).

For UI work with populated specs, statecharts, failures and recordings, run the separate examples target:

```sh
bun run workspace:preview
```

This viewer uses `examples/todo/specs` and the existing example-evidence adapter. It does not seed or
alter the real server's data. It has no server administration interface. Existing example run files are
shown when present; setup does not run browsers, model checkers or generate recordings. To create fresh
example recordings, use the existing `example:run` command and [statechart guide](statecharts.md).

## Shared commands

| Command | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `bun run workspace:setup` | Check the pinned Bun and install with `--frozen-lockfile`; safe to repeat. |
| `bun run workspace:run` | Run the real node and viewer; repeat the frozen install before starting. |
| `bun run workspace:preview` | Run the populated examples viewer; repeat the same setup first. |
| `bun run workspace:status` | Print live URLs, mode and readiness as JSON; omit private control credentials. |
| `bun run workspace:stop` | Stop both targets owned by this checkout; retain all reports. |
| `bun run workspace:stop server` | Stop only the API/viewer target. `preview` selects only examples. |
| `bun run workspace:check` | Run documentation, types, tests, package/client builds and consumer smoke. |

`run` and `preview` stay in the foreground so the IDE owns their lifetime and displays their output.
Ctrl+C or an IDE Stop closes the owned server and its child process. Teardown uses a random private
control capability stored in `.atlas-workspace/`; it never kills a PID from a file or uses `pkill`.
If the owned development child does not finish after five seconds, only that child is terminated.
Stopping an unrelated IDE, agent, checkout or application is outside these scripts' scope.

## Workspace isolation and ports

The API/viewer tries port 5180, and examples try 5181. If that default is busy, the OS supplies a free
port. Read `workspace:status` instead of assuming a URL. An explicit `--port`, `ATLAS_PORT`, or `PORT`
(in that priority order) is strict: conflicts fail and never connect publishers to a different node.
`--port 0` requests a free port explicitly.

```sh
bun run workspace:run --port 5280
bun run workspace:status
```

Everything binds to `127.0.0.1`. For remote workspaces, use the IDE's port forwarding. Reports and server
settings are kept in S3 only, never in the checkout: `workspace:run` needs the required `ATLAS_S3_*` variables
(copy `.env.example` to `.env`, which Bun loads, or export them) and exits at once, listing every missing one,
without them. Give each checkout its own bucket or `ATLAS_S3_PREFIX` if their reports must not mix
(`workspace:setup` and `workspace:preview` need no credentials). Live runtime leases stay in `.atlas-workspace/`.
Keep that directory private to each worktree. Do not share `node_modules`,
`.atlas-workspace/` or caches across checkouts with different dependencies. Frozen installs use Bun's
download cache without linking one worktree's dependency tree to another.

Two simultaneous starts cannot claim the same target's runtime lease. A hard kill may leave metadata:
run `workspace:stop` before restarting. It removes a stale lease only when its owner PID is gone; if the
PID is still alive but the control endpoint cannot authenticate, investigate that owner rather than
assuming it is safe to stop. No reports or settings are deleted by teardown.

## Superset

[`.superset/config.json`](https://github.com/crvouga/atlas/blob/main/.superset/config.json) wires workspace creation to setup, the Run button
to the real node/viewer, and teardown to stop. Superset discovers listening ports; the conventional
ports are labelled in [ports.json](https://github.com/crvouga/atlas/blob/main/.superset/ports.json). Automatically chosen ports still appear
in its port panel. Use the examples command in a second terminal when needed. Personal lifecycle
overrides belong in ignored `.superset/config.local.json`.

Superset's Run command resolves from the main repository's configuration. Commit the configuration
and scripts together before expecting another workspace's Run button to discover them. See the
[official lifecycle guide](https://docs.superset.sh/setup-teardown-scripts) and
[port management](https://docs.superset.sh/ports).

## super.engineering

[`.super.engineering/config.json`](https://github.com/crvouga/atlas/blob/main/.super.engineering/config.json) defines **Atlas** (default),
**Viewer examples** and **Checks** in the Run controls. Each server target's Stop command affects only
that target; deletion stops both. Shared commands expose **Atlas URLs**, **Check Atlas** and a
**Review Atlas UI** prompt. The prompt uses the current agent's configured provider and does not
launch a team or change model settings.

Use the documented CLI to inspect or invoke the same definitions:

```sh
sc project scripts check --json
sc project scripts run Atlas --json
sc project scripts status --json
sc project scripts stop Atlas --json
```

Edit shared script configuration with `sc project scripts set ... --scope repo`, and shared commands
with `sc commands ... --scope shared`. Preserve other entries and unknown configuration keys. See
[project config and scripts](https://super.engineering/docs/project-config-and-scripts/).

## Orca

[`orca.yaml`](https://github.com/crvouga/atlas/blob/main/orca.yaml) uses the supported `scripts.setup` and `scripts.archive` hooks. Agents
wait for setup. The first default tab is reserved for the agent; the second starts Atlas. Tab commands
may start alongside setup, so Run repeats the frozen install before importing application dependencies.
Orca's normal shared-script trust and setup-policy settings still apply. No `scripts.run` key is
invented: Orca starts the app through the terminal template.

Keep **Shared + Local** or **Shared only** enabled for repository hooks, and approve the shared config
in Orca when it offers its trust prompt. These are user-owned controls. For existing workspaces,
run the shared Bun commands in a terminal; default tabs are created for new workspaces. See the
[official `orca.yaml` reference](https://www.onorca.dev/docs/model/orca-yaml).

## Agent workflow

Read `AGENTS.md`, then use `workspace:status` to discover this checkout's live app. Run the server for
API, settings, upload and streaming changes; use examples for populated UI review. Read [UI conventions](ui.md)
before changing screens. Keep report/schema/permission contracts intact, and report what the browser and
checks actually verified. Do not launch other agents, change IDE permissions or install global IDE tooling
as a side effect of setup. `workspace:check` is an on-demand verification target, never a creation hook.

The lifecycle regression suite (`bun test scripts/workspace.test.ts`) checks fresh directories with spaces,
repeatable setup, strict ports, separate stores, authenticated ownership and independent shutdown.
Real IDE boot verification additionally needs that IDE installed and available; a passing configuration
test alone does not prove the IDE started a new workspace.
</doc>

<doc path="docs/ui.md">
# Viewer UI conventions

Read this before changing the Atlas viewer or settings UI. React and Mantine are the design system.
Use the installed version in `package.json` (currently 9.7.3) and its [official documentation](https://mantine.dev/).
Look up unfamiliar interactions before writing them; component props and compound components usually solve them.

## One setup

- `packages/visualizer/src/ui/theme.tsx` owns the only theme and `AtlasThemeProvider`.
- Both `src/main.tsx` (reports) and `src/admin/main.tsx` (settings) use that provider and Mantine's styles.
- Keep Atlas's blue navigation, neutral surfaces, system typography, and light color scheme. Outcome colors
  come from `statusColor`: green passed, red failed, orange flaky, blue running, gray unknown/unrun.
  Always accompany color with text or a named status mark. Unknown evidence must never look passed.
- The theme darkens the existing Mantine outcome scales and muted text to meet small-text contrast requirements. Use the default sizes, radii, font sizes, shadows and variants. Defaults belong in the theme, not in features.
  The spacing vocabulary is Mantine's `xs`, `sm`, `md`, `lg`, `xl`.

## Compose directly

Use `AppShell` for persistent navigation, `Container size="xl"` for report pages (`md` for settings),
`Stack` for vertical flow, `Group` for horizontal flow, and `SimpleGrid` for responsive metrics/forms.
Page headers contain a `Title order={1}`, descriptive `Text c="dimmed"`, then the page's controls.
Use `Title order={2}` for sections and `order={3}` for subsections; do not choose heading sizes per page.

Use Mantine components directly. Do not add wrappers for ordinary buttons, inputs, cards, menus, or dialogs.
Shared product compositions include `SpecHeader`, `ResultRow`, `StatusMark`, `Origin`, `Stage`, and `TestDetail`:
they preserve evidence semantics, provenance, URL selection, or playback behavior.

- Primary action: `Button variant="filled"`. Secondary: default `Button` (light). Quiet: `variant="subtle"`.
  Destructive action: `color="red"`. Icon-only action: `ActionIcon` with an `aria-label`, usually a `Tooltip`.
- Inputs: Mantine inputs with a visible `label`, `description` when needed, and `error` for validation.
  Use `NativeSelect` for small native option lists; keep form values controlled. Settings validation and
  authorization stay on the server; its optional JSON editor also validates with the shared schema.
- Use `Menu` for navigation menus, `Popover` for view options, `Drawer` for sources/test details,
  `Modal` for modal content, and `Spotlight` for search. Let Mantine own dismissal, focus and keyboard behavior.
  When an action opens a drawer from a popover, close and disable the parent popover during the drawer's lifetime;
  return focus to its persistent trigger. Do not fix overlapping focus traps by raising z-index values.
- Use `Tabs` for view modes and `Accordion` for disclosure. URL-backed selections stay in the existing router.
- Render typed router links with Mantine's `renderRoot={props => <Link {...props} ... />}`.
  This keeps route/search type inference and native navigation semantics.
- Use `Table` in `Table.ScrollContainer` for wide evidence, with column headers. Long lists must retain
  `Bounded`/show-more controls. Do not fetch unopened results' recordings eagerly.
- Loading: named `Loader`/`Skeleton` or explicit text with `role="status"`. Error: `Alert color="red"` and
  a retry when possible. Empty: descriptive `Text` and a relevant action. Use built-in loading/disabled states.
- Spec overview links use a centered `Group`: status, flexible title/folder, then outcome and time. Keep gaps
  explicit with theme spacing; stack metadata on narrow screens instead of crowding the title.

## Executable spec source

`SourceText` is the common source reader for Gherkin, Quint, DMN/XML, Alloy, OpenSLO/YAML and statechart
XML/JSON/YAML. Show it expanded near the top of document pages; preserve indentation, comments and the
complete file. Do not replace source with a trimmed snapshot. Mantine `CodeHighlightTabs` supplies file
labels, line numbers, horizontal scrolling and copying. The full file is expanded by default. Native
collapse/expand controls can limit long files to 70vh; the Recorded results action jumps to the existing
results section and moves keyboard focus there. Keep scenario selection,
filters, traces, decision tables and model declaration links working alongside the source.

`ui/highlight.ts` owns the one lazy Shiki adapter. It imports only the supported grammars and caches the
engine. The shared source composition installs that adapter when source is displayed; the Mantine theme
and component defaults still live only in `ui/theme.tsx`. Quint/Alloy grammar sources and licenses live in
[`ui/grammars/README.md`](../packages/visualizer/src/ui/grammars/README.md). Unknown formats remain plain
text, and parse failures must leave the source visible. Syntax highlighting never means a spec passed.

## Icons and notation marks

Use named imports from `@tabler/icons-react` for all UI glyphs. The icon package supplies SVG paths;
Mantine still supplies every control and interaction. Use size 16 for compact inline glyphs and size 20
for standalone actions, with `aria-hidden="true"` when the adjacent text or control names the action.
Do not draw SVG icons, use Unicode glyphs as buttons, or add another icon library. Mantine's built-in
icons are fine. Keep textual keyboard shortcuts and path separators as text.

`SpecLogo` maps every `SpecKind` to a bundled SVG mark, used in navigation and page headers. Keep the
visible notation label; marks are decorative. Sources, licenses and the DMN notation-mark choice are in
[`spec-logos/README.md`](../packages/visualizer/src/components/spec-logos/README.md). Add a sourced SVG
and update this mapping when adding a format. Brand artwork preserves upstream colors independently of
Atlas's theme. SVG data plots and statechart arrow markers are geometry, not handcrafted UI icons.

## Accessibility and responsive behavior

The shell collapses its index below Mantine's `md` breakpoint; its named Burger toggles mobile navigation.
Navigation closes after choosing a destination. Use responsive props and the theme's breakpoints; no custom
media-query system. Let controls wrap, use one form column on mobile, and keep dialogs inside the viewport.
Wide tables scroll inside their container. Native video/audio controls remain available.

Preserve labels, status announcements, keyboard shortcuts, selected states, meaningful headings and focus
restoration. Mantine respects reduced motion through the central theme. Avoid nested interactive controls.
Never rely on color alone, remove focus outlines, or hide an important action only to make a layout fit.

## Styling policy and exceptions

Default custom CSS: zero. First try Mantine defaults, central defaults, variants, props, layout components,
and theme tokens. Do not add Tailwind, Radix, another design system, CSS modules, custom token scales,
inline styles, or `styles` objects for ordinary UI. Document a concrete functional limitation here before
adding an exception; `scripts/ui-architecture.test.ts` checks these boundaries in the normal test suite.

The central List Styles API adjustment makes item labels fill the available width, including Mantine's column wrappers;
List has no full-width label prop. This keeps all report rows usable without feature styles.

The narrowly scoped exceptions are:

1. **Interactive statechart graph:** React Flow and ELK provide graph layout, pan/zoom, edges and minimap,
   which Mantine does not supply. Graph nodes and controls use Mantine. `src/map/map.module.css` only covers
   SVG strokes, graph handles, edge-label geometry and graph selection/dimming. The two edge-label transforms
   and node dimensions are computed by the layout engine, not visual design tokens.
2. **Captured evidence:** native video/audio and sandboxed iframes render recorded bytes. HTML snapshots use
   the existing isolated shadow tree and intrinsic phone coordinates; their captured styles never style Atlas.
   Recorded click markers and intrinsic image/video dimensions are evidence coordinates, not UI spacing.
3. **Public compatibility APIs:** `solid-js` and `@tanstack/solid-query` remain dependencies of existing
   report-library entry points. They render no Atlas screen. Do not import them into the viewer or add Solid UI.
4. **Syntax rendering:** Shiki is the syntax engine behind Mantine's official code-highlight adapter,
   not a second component system. Its token styles and escaped HTML are generated by the highlighter.
   The supported Shiki line transformer supplies the existing Quint `line-N` navigation anchors.
   No feature CSS, handcrafted code controls or custom syntax color theme is introduced.
5. **Consumer test fixture:** `examples/todo/app` is the app Atlas tests and records, not an Atlas screen.
   Its intentionally separate implementation and selectors are test inputs; the overhaul does not restyle it.

## Inventory and migration boundary

| Area | Screens/interactions | Mantine composition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shared shell | Project switching, spec navigation, run selection, connection status, diagnostics, mobile index | AppShell, Burger, NavLink, Menu, Popover, NativeSelect, Drawer |
| Project home | Tests/runs tabs, metrics, search, status/environment/domain filters, grouping, sorting, show more | Container, Tabs, SimpleGrid, Paper, TextInput, Button, Accordion |
| Test detail | Current outcomes, statistics, duration graph, history, artifacts, recording; the `layer` address parameter pins it to one run's result, labelled "This run" against "Latest combined evidence" | Drawer, Table, Badge, Alert, Stage |
| Specs | All six existing kinds, overview/index, Gherkin rules/scenarios/examples, Quint declarations/traces, DMN tables, source text | SpecHeader, Accordion, Table, CodeHighlightTabs, ResultRow |
| Statecharts | Graph, screen/event/journey details, developer metadata, chart test results | Mantine cards/navigation and product compositions; graph exception above |
| Evidence | Steps, retries, annotations, facts, unknown extensions, safe downloads and previews | List, Badge, Accordion, Code, Image, native media |
| Recordings | Pictures/video/timeline, actor selection, moments, failure jumps, timing, model-state differences | Tabs, Slider, Button, ScrollArea, Table, Progress |
| Search/help | Ranked and semantic search, shortcut help, recording shortcuts | Spotlight, Modal, Kbd |
| Administration | Token access, S3 storage notice, garbage collection policy (saved in S3), live timeouts, report rules, limits, raw JSON, conflicts | Same provider/theme, Fieldset, Mantine inputs, Accordion, Alert |

The hash routes (`/`, `/chart/$chartId`, `/specs/$kind`), query contracts, project scoping, streaming,
report APIs and data adapters remain the migration boundary. `/admin` still serves an independent document:
